column5: o Activities which comprise application of the Sub-National DeMPA methodology are focused on understanding local practices/procedures covering some 15 debt management performance indicators (DPIs), which span the full range of debt management functions. Procedures and policies are contrasted-- through the use of detailed criteria for performance 'ratings' - with sound international practice, and a grading is assigned to each of the DPIs. The DeMPA process is a highly interactive one, with in-depth discussion of issues being the primary means through which understanding of debt management practices are reached. In addition to the DMO, the team also meets with management of other departments within the Ministry of Finance, Treasury, the Central Bank, Auditor General, and other Government agencies which interact with DMO to help with the assessment- as well as with private sector players (e.g. commercial banks, other investors) to understand 'client' views of practices, notably in the area of the functioning of domestic markets.   o In technical terms, an Agenda and required meetings for the mission are pre-arranged with the client-- with changes to the overall Agenda made as additional areas for exploration come to light-- or particular issues of concern suggest that additional time be allocated. The team will prepare a preliminary assessment of debt management practices during the mission, and present initial conclusions at a wrap-up session-- including suggestions for next-steps in the process of improving practices in the DMO through additional TA or other means. A full draft report for consideration by the client will be prepared upon return to office- and following iteration on comments and suggestions- a final report will be submitted to the authorities.Regarding key issues for DeMPA- and indirectly, for the medium term development objective of improving capacity and performance of debt management activities:o the DeMPA process should be comprehensive and transparent o assessments of performance on DPIs should reflect the consensus of the World Bank team, given the criteria in the DeMPA Guidance Noteo initial and final reports should be peer reviewed for quality and the clarity/foundations for assessmentso response to client questions/concerns as well as preparation of reports should be timely and of high quality

column5: In order to provide an appropriate empirical analysis that combines urban economics and private sector analytics, the work will draw on staff and analytical frameworks from both SDN and FPD within the Bank.  From SDN the framework developed through Urbanization Review country pilots (utilized from 2007 until now in Brazil, China, Colombia, Georgia, Ghana, India, Turkey and Vietnam) will be applied.  From FPD techniques that are customarily used to assess national and regional competitiveness will be utilized.  The team to conduct this work will be drawn jointly from AFR SDN, AFR FPD, SDN Urban Anchor, and FPD Competitive Industries Practice.The study will focus on assessing the following:?	Nigeria?s spatial and demographic transition will explore the relationship between urbanization, rural-urban linkages, and economic growth at the local, regional, and national levels.?	The urban economic development assessment will assess which enterprises, markets and industries are generating jobs and economic growth?and how this varies by size of city.  It will scan emergent value chains, including in informal settlements with special attention to be given to economic linkages among Lagos, second tier cities, small towns and rural villages.?	An assessment of urban institutions will include looking at institutions regulating factor markets and the delivery of basic services as the foundations for high quality urbanization.  This will also include bottlenecks in housing markets, focusing on five vulnerabilities: affordability, legal rights, financial innovation, supporting infrastructure, and opportunities for income.?	The infrastructure assessment will focus on mobility and connectivity considering city competitiveness and transport connectivity for international, inter-urban and intra-urban trade movements.The units of analysis will be: (i) 774 Local Government Areas, (ii) 36 States and one Federal Capital Territory, or (iii) 6 geopolitical zones depending on data availability.  The analyses will draw on some reuse and reinterpretation of existing data and analyses, and also considerable secondhand data collection with some new analyses.  These analyses will be benchmarked with the prior Urbanization Reviews and private sector development analyses.  The primary benchmark will be a large economy, federal systems with abundant natural resources, such as Brazil and India, which will shed light on a set of policy options which have been tested to be effective in a country comparable to Nigeria.The team will seek to understand what visions and strategies currently exist among policymakers for Lagos, second tier cities, small towns and rural villages and what policy options are being implemented to achieve these visions.  This step will be undertaken at the same time as a perceptions survey of firms in specific value chains about city-level constraints on growth, and a number of focus groups at which conclusions of the preceding analysis are presented and discussed.The team will produce a set of suggestions on policy options in order for Nigeria to achieve successful urbanization, economic growth, and balanced regional development in coming years.  This will include, and may even highlight, issues of political economy and institutions.  For example, in terms of land and housing markets, we will review existing relevant policies and regulations that may limit the fluidity of land markets, where valuation of land is a key component, and seek to understand the challenges in terms of coordinated policies for land management and infrastructure provision, including transport.

column5: The proposed Program Development Objective (PDO)of the Nigeria green belt corridors development program is to improve transport and trade connectivity and facilitate market integration along Nigeria?s key economic corridors.  This is a multi-sectoral complex and long-term undertaking that requires adopting a multiphase programmatic instrument/approach (MPA).  The Government of Nigeria (GON) has requested financing for the improvement of critical road infrastructure and logistics services along the economic corridors spread in the gateway states, south eastern region, north western region and River Nile corridor. The request includes 23 road projects with a total length of about 2,400km.  The investment requirement for the urban renewal is anticipated to be high. Private investment is required to operationalize the SEZs and establish commodity exchange centers.  Therefore, the proposed program will be implemeted in phases.  This MPA will support an integrated approach to economic corridor development with a focus on: i) upgrading priority transport corridors at the national and sub-national levels; ii) improving logistics infrastructure and services; and iii) creating an enabling environment for private investment.Phase 1 will focus on improving priority transport corridors at the national and sub-national levels, whilst developing the interventions that will support the economic transformation by addressing key regulatory gaps along the economic corridors. Phases 2 and 3 will expand the support for spatial transformation and regional economic integration through the development of economic development corridors and other complementary interventions with multi-sectoral interventions at national and sub-national levels.

column5: Nigeria: TA on Community Broadcasting Development    1.  Background -- Rationale for Bank's Interest.   Within WBI's support to media development in Nigeria, WBI and the Country Department have agreed that starting in FY06, WBI will provide technical assistance to support the development of independent public interest broadcasting.  The focus for that effort would be on community radio development.  Community radio is being given special attention because it has proved to be a sustainable and interactive medium for poor and illiterate populations to be heard, be informed, shape knowledgeable opinions, learn the give-and-take of informed dialogue, and become more decisive agents in their own development.  Local news and educational programs can greatly enhance transparency, a cornerstone of democracy and way to thwart corruption. The end result can be stronger, more effective and appropriate development activities. By helping poor constituencies to develop their own local news programs and to present discussions on matters affecting their community, community radio broadcasting not only helps poor people to share information in a language they understand, but also fosters debate on issues, facilitates access to government decision meetings and events, and helps community members to organize themselves to identify, and benefit from more opportunities.    As has happened in quite a number of developing countries, when the Nigerian government  liberalized its media regime and withdrew from its monopoly over the airwaves, it treated this process as a straight privatization task.  That is, it opened the airwaves to commercial braodcasters but did not take account of the public goods nature of the radiofrequency spectrum and the need to provision a portion of the spectrum to non-profit public service uses.  Good practice internationally in terms of broadcasting legislation and regulation recognizes that there are three major broadcasting sectors: government financed public service broadcasting, commercial broadcasting, and community broadcasting which is independent, non-profit and focused on local development issues.    We are finding that community broadcasting provides an extremely good entry point for pluralistic and informative media development.  Its focus is on community programming development on issues important to the community members themselves.  Such stations operate in local languages, are non-sectarian, non-partisan, and non-profit.  And they have proven to be sustainable, largely because of they rely on extremely strong ownership and commitment of the commmunities they serve.  Community radio stations have been operating for over 50 years in Latin America.  In Africa, they began to emerge in the 1980s/90s.  In Mali there are over 200 community radio stations that are thriving.  In Ghana, the community radio sector is still small (due to problems in the enabling environment), but it is vibrant and includes a national network of community radio stations (the Ghana Community Radio Network).  In fact, the operations of the Ghanaian stations, and the services provided by GCRN represent in many ways, the 'gold standard' in Africa.    Community radio is a tool for poverty reduction, and strengthens awareness and sustained pressures on government to be accountable.    2.  Key Elements of Bank Assistance.   Through our support in diverse countries and regions, we can see the importance of providing assistance at the policy and regulatory level and at the grassroots institutional and capacity-building level.   Usually this includes an assessment of the enabling environment with recommendations of critically important reforms, and in parallel, technical assistance in prototyping genuine community radio stations, embedded in Bank operations.  The latter provides concreteness for decision-makers about what community broadcasting is, what's required for it to function, and demonstrates to those removed from  the grassroots that there is capacity in poor communities to run these stations to serve the local communities' needs.  It also demystifies CR for Bank staff and clarifies how best to support CR development, to ensure genuine commitment and ownership by poor constituencies, and to strengthen poor people's 'capacity to engage,'  including in calling officials to account and negotiating improvements in public services.  The policy dialogue can include direct participation from poor communities, and usually requires domestic coalition-building based on interests already at play.   Tactics need to be very context specific, with domestic constituencies in the lead and the Bank supporting.  Hence, starting by engaging the constituencies and organizations that are already pressing for sustained development of the community broadcasting sector in Nigeria is crucial. In Nigeria, work has been underway for at least a year to build a broad coalition advocating reforms to enable community radio sector development.  This effort is being coordinated by the Institute for Media and Society (IMS), in collaboration with AMARC (the World Association of Community Radio Broadcasters) and Panos.  Their work to date has included 1.   regional awareness raising meetings that have been well attended and connect this initiative with wider constituencies; 2.   development of a stakeholders' charter (by IMS/AMARC/Panos), called Road Map to Building a Sustainable Community Radio Sector in Nigeria,  that provides background, the state of play and goals; 3.   a National Validation Seminar on Building Community Radio in Nigeria, held in Abuja on April 5-7, 2005.  This meeting produced a communique of specific  recommendations for reforms and other improvements in the enabling environment; 4.   An Action Plan for Community Radio Development, produced at the Abuja validation seminar.  This includes actions to strengthen a)   advocacy and awareness  with government executive agencies, parliament, regulatory agencies, groups that have submitted applications for CR licenses, grassroots communities, the media, academia, Nigerian equipment producers, international development organizations, research and training institutions, and West African broadcast regulatory bodies; b)   empowerment and capacity-building which focuses on the development of community radio pilots; and c)   monitoring, networking and communication regarding the effort as a whole. Technical assistance will be provided to this coalition of stakeholders, coordinated by IMS, beginning with a core group of participants in the Abuja seminar.  It will include support to the policy dialogue with  the National Broadcasting Corporation and other key government players and for participatory development of community radio prototyping in Fadama, a nation-wide CDD project that has strong popular and government support.  The activity will begin with a stakeholders' consultation meeting in Lagos, to 1.   discuss the reform proposals and action plan noted above, and the context; 2.   get a sense of the prioritization and sequencing of reforms that could be considered; 3.   clarify what background analyses of the enabling environment IMS/AMARC/Panos have done, itemize the laws and regulations that we will need to review, and assess what further analysis may be required; 4.   clarify the extent to which common ground has already been built with the National Broadcasting Corporation and other key government players, and 5.   glean these stakeholders' views on issues we should raise with NBC and other government actors, and prepare ourselves. column5: Two important issues were flagged in the conclusions of the previous Poverty work program and during the review meeting discussion. First, Nigeria needs to substantially improve the quality and quantity of socio economic statistics. GHS together with the Demographic and Health Survey turned out to be the only reasonable socio-economic dataset available in the country. Most of the other datasets presented several flaws; three types of problems have surfaced during the analysis that need attention: (i) data quality issues, requiring several rounds of cleaning of data-sets (ii) poor documentation and archiving that prevented the use of several rounds of the GHS cross sections, especially for producing statistics at the national level using population weights and (iii) comparability, permitting the comparisons of key variables of interest over time, tracking the impact of policy and other events. Second, the size and diversity of the country requires more focused analysis whereas the NPWP painted a broad-brush picture at national level. In particular the Northern region performance requires an ad hoc analysis given the renewed engagement of the World Bank in the area. An analysis on Northern regions should focus on the particular socio economic and climatic conditions faced in that area. Problems such as agricultural markets fragmentation, the relative low level of many public services (e.g. education, health and infrastructures), gender discrimination, the high proneness to price and climatic shocks of Northern farmers and the ongoing conflicts need to be tackled with an ad hoc analysis.Moreover, in a scenario in which almost two thirds of the Nigerian poor seem to reside in the North where most of recent conflicts took place, the link between conflicts and poverty cannot be overlooked. Conflicts represent a serious threat to the political and social stability of several Northern states; at present, however, no quantitative analysis has so far assessed their socio-economic impact.The current work program builds on recent findings from NPWP FY14-15. It sets out to address requests that emerged during the review process with a comprehensive framework combining Technical Assistance to NBS, construction of a Poverty and Conflict monitoring system for Northern Nigeria and production of the Northern Nigeria Poverty and Conflicts Report. column5: To generate knowledge and inform investment decision making on livestock system resilience building in Northern Nigeria.The in-depth assessment of CSA intervention options will build on a literature review of existing analytical work, quantitatively model costs and benefits of packages of intervention options at micro and macro levels following established analytical approaches and review international experience to derive lessons learned and international best practice to generate an improved evidence base for investment decision making. Special emphasis will be placed on understanding and addressing the intersection between livestock system resilience and conflicts between herders and farmers in the North as well as in the Middle belt and the South. The process will be underpinned by continuous stakeholder involvement, extensive in-country research in collaboration with local partners and contextualization within the relevant national strategy and policy frameworks. As a result, client decision making capacity will be strengthened and the development of the upcoming investment operation Livestock Productivity and Resilience Support Project (P160865) informed. The activity also serves as a pilot of a new analytical instrument for the Agriculture GP: Climate Smart Investment Plans (CSIP). CSIPs build on the successful CSA profiles. Where the profiles provided an overview of CSA at the country level and offered a long list of promising CSA technologies, CSIPs will take the analysis one step further to generate concrete intervention options with quantified cost/benefit profiles to inform investment decision making. The CSIP methodology is currently under development. This activity provides an opportunity to test methodological approaches and derive lessons learned in a continuous feedback loop between pilot and methodology development.

column5: The objective of activity was to integrate violence and crime prevention into the planning and implementation of urban upgradingprojects, as well as in the overall policy making process in Edo State.  Edo State requested the support from the World Bank for their First State Development Policy Operation (Edo DPO-1). As the first ina planned series of three annual operations aimed at supporting policy and institutional reforms in the implementation of the StateGovernment's development strategy - Edo Vision 2020, the Edo DPO-1 is focused on improving fiscal and public financial management,urban development and investment climate. A lack of systematic planning and oversight, coupled with extremely high prevalence ofcrime and violence, especially in Benin City (State capital of Edo State) undermine development efforts. These challenges areparticularly difficult in the last two areas of focus under the State. For these reasons, the State  expressed the need to learn from other countries where ICT platforms were used to integrate citizens'feedback and geo-reference empirical information into the planning and implementation of urban development projects, as well as in the overall policy making process in large urban settlements.  Due to the interest raised by the exchange among participants (Government officials, CSOs, and academia members), stakeholders inBenin City requested assistance from the Bank in designing and implementing a pilot project to address crime and violenceprevention integrating the key aspects of mechanisms presented in the exchange (improvement of data gathering and managementmechanisms on urban upgrading and crime and violence; multi-sectoral decision making and coordinated policy action; citizenparticipation in identification of risks and oversight of responses and prevention efforts through urban upgrading projects).  This pilot was designed on a South-South cooperation principle, through which experiences and expertise of technical advisers fromother countries with similar experiences, including Latin America, were used by the team as inputs for the design andimplementation of activities.  From July 4 to 8, 2011 over 43 representatives of Edo State Government, as well as representativesof civil society organizations, and academia took place, in Benin City (Edo State) a South-South Exchange (SSE) on thetopicparticipated in a Conference on & 65533;Urban Upgrading for Violence Prevention& 65533; in Benin City.  Also, pilot' activities that aim to strengthened the capacity of the Edo State Police to collect and process crime and violence data included the participation of a consultant from Latin America with extensiveexperience in the area of crime and violence prevention in the LAC region. Other consultants who  participated in the design of thepilot have ample experience in a range of projects for crime and violence prevention initiatives in Colombians. Their experience and expertise was integrated into the pilot design process to continue building on the south-south experiencesexchanged during the first phase of this project and supporting the transference of knowledge between Colombia and Nigeria.

column5: This is continuation of the recently completed work on the preparation of the federal PEMFAR, isa consolidated diagnostic tool designed to enhance the Bank's, Development partners' and member countries' knowledge of PFM arrangements and reform challenges. The PEMFAR intends to cover the tasks that have been traditionally undertaken by separate Bank reports such as public expenditure reviews (PER), country financial accountability assessment (CFAA), and country procurement assessment Review (CPAR). The second stage of the PEMFAR work will largely cover several additional states to inform Bank policy dialogue with the respective state governments and Bank operational work. It will also include some additional sectoral work, in sectors such as agriculture and roads. The analysis will be based on in-depth review of (i) regulatory framework, government programs, and business processes in the PFM area, (ii) data on approved and executed government budgets, (iii) fiscal data collected from specially commissioned surveys, and (iv) findings and data gathered under the ongoing Bank and DFID projects. Assessment of Nigerian fiscal management systems and processes will be done against the PEFA performance management framework (PEFA, 2005), which would (i) provide an important comparative cross-country perspective on Nigerian assessment, and (ii) help identify some binding constraints within the existing PFM system and thus better prioritize the recommendations. This PEFA-type assessment is planned for both federal and state government levels. The expenditure data analysis will be undertaken against government policy priorities as reflected in the NEEDS and will be aimed to advise the FGN on better alignment of expenditure policies with the NEEDS and MDGs. It is also expected that the PEMFAR preparation will conclude with an agreement with the participating states on a medium term action plan that would reflect core PEMFAR recommendations, put them into a broader context of government reforms in Nigeria, and establish a clear link to donor support of the agreed reforms.

column5: Project Objective: This project is part of a multi-country program and will contribute to a key public good: the global eradication of Poliomyelitis by 2005 as aimed for by the World Health Organization.The overall goal of this project is to assist Nigeria in its efforts to eradicate Poliomyelitis.  More specifically, the objective of this supplemental credit is to provide the additional polio vaccine required to carry out the intensification of Nigeria's ongoing polio eradication program during 2005 and 2006, needed because of the outbreaks of wild polio especially in but not limited to the North of the country.Key Performance Indicators: The project.s success would be measured by the following key indicators and targets:·   Timely arrival at national level of OPV procured through UNICEF. Target: vaccines arrive at least 5 weeks before the SIA in the national strategic store in Abuja. Tool: UNICEF/NPI vaccine arrival report.·   Coverage of SIA. Target: coverage of OPV is at least 80% in each endemic State. Tool: cluster sample survey according to a WHO approved methodology.Achievements measured by these indicators will be decisive for the IDA buy-down.Project description: The on-going IDA supported PPEP has three components: (i) the procurement of OPV; (ii) supplemental operations including cold chain, social mobilization and training; and (iii) surveillance.  IDA finances the first component. The project is part of a multi-donor financed framework which has provided funding amounting US $ 157.1 million, of which IDA financed US $ 28.7 million for procurement of OPV.Rationale for the Supplemental CreditNigeria.s polio initiative is guided by ERC, a group comprised of global and national polio experts. Based on review of the surveillance data in August 2004, ERG concluded that Nigeria is making poor progress and is not on track to achieve polio eradication by 2005.  Therefore, ERC recommended to intensify SIA efforts during 2004 and 2005.  FGN and the ICC have endorsed the recommendations to intensify SIAs and have initiated actions to implement them.The proposed Supplemental Credit would finance the procurement of extra OPV required for additional SIAs in 2005.  The proposed credit is consistent with the original project development objective and meets the requirement of OP13.20 on supplemental financing

column311: Operation Abstract: Summary Description of Proposed OperationNigeria DARES is envisioned as a scalable platform for achieving universal electrification and supporting energy transition through private sector investment. The platform aims to provide ? (i) basic electrification (multiple lighting, radio, and mobile phone charging ability) to over 13 million unserved, rural, and remote Nigerians through the deployment of standalone solar, and (ii) grid equivalent electrification via mini grid to over 2.7 million Nigerians, in rural and peri urban settings. The platform will also support Nigeria?s clean energy transition by increasing the reliability of electricity supply for 1.3 million existing electricity consumers, in peri urban and urban areas, by connecting them to cleaner and more reliable interconnected mini grids that will help replace approximately 288,000 diesel/gasoline gensets. The platform will also support the electrification of federal and state public institutions, such as healthcare and educational facilities, with distributed renewable energy (DRE) under an energy-as-a-service business model to crowd in private sector investment and ensure sustainable operation and maintenance (O&M). The platform will also provide an estimated 237,000 micro, small and medium enterprises (including around 124,000 agri-businesses) with reliable and clean electricity for productive uses that will help improve their economic output, create local jobs, and improve the financial sustainability of mini grids. The focus of the program is on scaling up mini grids and SAS deployment in Nigeria.The project supports the following components:Component 1. Solar Hybrid Mini Grids for Economic Development will support the development of privately owned and operated solar hybrid mini grids in unserved (primarily rural and remote) and underserved (primarily urban and peri-urban) areas that have high economic growth potential. It will also support the electrification of public institutions at the federal and sub-national level such as healthcare and educational facilities. The mini grid component consists of two investment sub-components defined by the different approaches they follow and will be implemented in parallel: Sub-component 1.1- the minimum subsidy tender and sub-component 1.2- performance-based grant program.Component 2: Standalone Solar Systems (SAS) for Households, MSMEs, and agribusinesses will expand availability and affordability of standalone solar systems (SAS) for households, MSMEs, and agribusinesses in rural areas. Through targeted and competitively awarded performance based grants, the uptake of 2,750,000 quality-certified solar home systems (SHS) and 75,000 PUE products in rural areas and amongst lower income segments will be promoted. Furthermore, solar solutions will be provided under an energy-as-a-service business model targeting MSMEs, economic clusters such as markets, plazas, trading centres, and agro-processing zones. Under the component, the Performance Based Grants (PBG) will provide results-based payments per connection. Component 3. Technical Assistance will support the creation of a framework for rural electrification upscaling, support project implementation, as well as broad capacity building at REA, NERC, FMPWH and other relevant stakeholders. It includes three sub-components: Institutional Strengthening and Policy Reform, Supporting DARES Ecosystem and Implementation, and Supporting States to Develop Solar Rooftop Ecosystem

column5: Task DescriptionAn Integrated Natural Resources Management Program for Nigeria: Key Issues and OptionsThe Terms of ReferenceThe following are the Terms of Reference for a desk study to develop 'A national natural resources management (NRM) program forNigeria' The NRM program will be implemented within the context of a Nigerian National Sustainable Rural development program.BackgroundThe Nigerian government, the World Bank and other partners have proposed the development of a national NRM program for Nigeria,that will ensure improved efficiency in the use of the national land , water and air resources for sustainable rural developmentand environmental protection. The program further seeks to promote appropriate measures for the maintenance and conservation of thequality of these important resources.The current set of practices for the management of these resources vary according to the contemporary land use  and agriculturalproduction systems, land tenure systems, socio-cultural practices, socio-economic realities, and the edicts, laws, legislation andordinances enacted by national authorities. Management of these resources are also subject to the dictates of local andinternational natural resource conservation conventions, the majority of which are improperly adopted and applied. Two major studies conducted under the EMP indicated major changes in the Nigerian landscape.  One study showed major changes inland use triggered by high rate of population growth and migration; and the other study indicated a net loss of approximately $ 60million a year on agricultural production due to soil degradation.There is currently increased awareness by the Federal Government of natural resource and environmental degradation. This isreflected in the 1988 Decree which established the Federal Environment Protection Agency (FEPA), the decree on the Natural ResourceConservation Council, 1989 (which later was merged with FEPA), and the establishing of an Ecological Fund.Development ObjectiveTo develop an integrated natural resource management program for Nigeria that focuses on priority areas taking into considerationthe needs of the main stakeholders as well as the economic, social and ecological values associated with the resource base.Strategic ObjectivesThe Specific ObjectivesThe specific objectives of the proposed Nigerian National NRM Issues Paper are as follows:1. To undertake a systematic review of the contents of a wide range of existing studies/reports covering NRM issues in Nigeria andthe recommendations therein (inter alia, Towards the development of an Environmental Action Plan for Nigeria, 1990, Nigeria Soiland Water management, 1989, Nigeria Land Resources Management Study, 1990, Vegetation and Land Use Changes in Nigeria, 1998,Assessment of Soil Degradation in Nigeria, 1998, An Environment and Development Strategy for the Niger Delta two Volumes);2. Identify the strategic issues related to the role of NRM in sustainable agriculture and sustainable rural development;specifically those related to (i) land tenure; (ii) land use; (iii) land capability and suitability; (iv) land degradation; (v)cropping systems; (vi) forest resources; (vii) biodiversity; (viii) fisheries and aquaculture; (ix) livestock; (x) water resources;(xi) gender issues; (xii) local capacities; (xiii) institutional frameworks;(xiv) participatory decision making;3. Identify options for preserving biodiversity and managing pollution impacts through the international waters window of theGEF.Here special emphasis will be on the Niger delta - in view of the fact that the delta is an area that needs special focus, andin order to respond to the needs of the government and of the communities.4. To identify the strategic technical, institutional and policy priorities relating to the development of a sustainablecommunity-based national NRM program;5. To examine linkages between economic and institutional policies and natural resource management and illustrate the role thatthese policies may play in sustainable natural resource management;6. To identify areas where specific programs and projects could be developed in pursuit of sustainable natural resourcesmanagement; and7. To identify areas where community-based natural resources management systems could be developed and where local knowledge, normsand institutions could evolve over time. Such community based natural resource management regimes are often found to be wellattuned to the local environment.The consultant will conduct a desk study to achieve objectives 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 above, and will submit a written report (theIssues and Options  Paper) summarizing the results of the desk study.The study will be conducted within the premises of the headquarters of the World Bank in Washington DC, and the Issues Paper shouldbe completed and submitted within 14 days of the commencement of the consultancy.Task DescriptionMajor conclusions/recommendations

Data will be collected by a combination of multi-sector field assessments, desk reviews, aerial reconnaissance, site visits by sector specialists, satellite imagery interpretation, and interviews with stakeholders. The assessment will build on the ongoing humanitarian assessment and will have the following three phases: ?	Preparatory and Desk Review Phase - including initial desk reviews to collect baseline information, determine the scope of the respective sector-wide reviews, identify information gaps, prepare data collection templates, and identify and rapidly hire field data collection consultants.  To begin with, desk reviews will be carried out to analyze and compile all available baselines information for the various sectors, to identify gaps in baseline data, and to also identify various data sources for the collection of both baseline and damage data.  ?	Analytical Work and Sector Strategic Reviews - When most of the damage data is available, sector teams will be mobilized to visit the affected areas to consult with provincial/district authorities, public/community representatives, NGOs, UN agencies, and other stakeholders, as well as examine the extent of the damage.  The teams will subsequently review the data provided by the government to assess the extent and quality of data available.  This will be followed by review and analysis of the data by sectoral/core teams to prepare the draft sector reports including impact, damage, loss and needs.  The Macro-economic and Human development expert team will then aggregate the sector specific results into the macro-economic analysis and human development impact and write-up.?	Final consultations and Report writing :  On completion of data collection and analysis, the sector teams will write sector report and cross team consultations and consultations with key stakeholders will be held to prioritize recovery strategies and costs. Other details work like ensuring that cross cutting issues are addressed and double counting is avoided will be done before the report is finalized. column4: Malaria Booster Project IE - CDD & PMV
column5: The US$180 million World Bank-assisted Malaria Control Booster Project (MCBP) became effective in May 2007 with the objectives of (i) ensuring that the target population in the project states have access to, and utilize, a well-defined set of Malaria Plus Package interventions (see highlighted below) and (ii) strengthening Federal- and State-level ability to manage and oversee the delivery of these interventions. An additional credit of US$100 million was approved in June 2009 to respond to the then recently updated National Malaria Strategy, specifically to the move towards universal coverage of the population with key malaria prevention and treatment interventions and the greater emphasis placed on diagnostics and health systems development.Two new interventions were proposed under the Community Systems Strengthening (CSS) Component of the Additional Financing (2009) as novel service-delivery channels to complement the delivery of publicly-funded malaria-related services through public primary healthcare facilities. These are: (i) Community-Directed Interventions, in which Community-Directed Distributors (CDDs) are trained to provide malaria control services to members of their extended families; and (ii) training Patent Medicine Vendors (PMVs) ? private drug retailers ? in diagnosis of malaria and the appropriate sale of subsidized Artemisinin-based Combination Therapies (ACTs). The CDD and PMV interventions were implemented from April 2013 to March 2015.This Impact Evaluation (IE) uses a cluster-randomized controlled trial design to test the effectiveness of CDD and PMV interventions. Randomization ensures that different groups of clusters are identical on average, in terms of both observed and unobserved characteristics, which creates a very strong basis for estimating the impact of one or more interventions. This activity was designed in collaboration with the Anambra State Malaria Control Booster Project, the Gombe State Malaria Control Booster Project, and the National Malaria Control Booster Project in order to estimate the causal impact, jointly and in isolation, of the CDD and PMV interventions in improving malaria-related preventive and care-seeking behavior and, consequently, in reducing the health and socioeconomic burden of malaria.

column5: The WASH Poverty Diagnostic will address a set of four core questions (CQ) relevant for Nigeria?s sub-sectors of both urban and rural water, sanitation and hygiene. (CQ-1) Who and where are the poor and bottom 40 percent of national distribution (consumption)?  Addressing this question is fundamental to identifying the populations of interest and will be done in close collaboration with the Poverty GP team who prepared the recent Nigeria Poverty Assessment, ensuring optimal use of human and financial resources. Building on the Nigeria Economic Report in 2014 based on General Household Surveys (GHS) conducted in 2010/2011 and 2012/2013,  the work will be coordinated with the Poverty GP to ensure synergies and avoid duplication of work, especially on core research questions 1 and 2. Throughout the work, focus will be kept on determining answers to the four CQs that are operationally and immediately relevant for the GoN, the World Bank and other development partners as well as the poor and bottom 40 percent themselves. (CQ-2) What is the level of access and quality of WASH services experienced by the poor and bottom 40 percent as compared to the non-poor and top 60 percent? The WASH diagnostic will use the same surveys used in CQ1 as well as two sets of surveys from a nationwide study commissioned by the Federal Ministry of Water Resources in 2015 to review the National Baseline Survey that was carried out in 2006/2007. Three indicators will be examined in particular: (i) the main source of drinking water for the household, (ii) the main type of toilet for the household, and (iii) as a proxy indicator for hand washing practices, the presence of hand washing facilities with soap and water. However the availability of data related to the quality of services, or ?access plus? as presented in the table below, is limited.  The DHS surveys provide insights on the types of infrastructure being used, such as whether water is accessed from a piped system or unprotected source or if latrines are considered ?improve? (hygienic and functional) or ?unimproved?.  Some surveys provide further insights into distance from water points and some household perceptions on water quantity and quality.  (CQ-3) What are the linkages and synergies between WASH and other sectors? Inadequate WASH alone does not cause poverty, but its synergies with other sectors can cause poor human development outcomes and exacerbate cycles of poverty. Targeting public investment for WASH to poor communities with high burden of WASH-related disease can create positive externalities for household health, and is an investment in human capital. (CQ-4) What are the WASH service-delivery constraints and potential solutions to improving services to the poor and bottom 40 percent? Addressing this question will require the use of multiple methods, from a desk review to quantitative and qualitative data, collected from key high poverty areas with substantial WASH access and quality problems. This will include qualitative surveys with service providers as well as with households and members of community organizations, where they exist in order to identify both demand and supply constraints in the delivery system. The data will also provide a ?real world? analysis of the key constraints to WASH for people at different points along the consumption distribution, and will be focused around four sub-questions:i.	What are constraints to WASH service delivery in general? ii.	Which of these have a particular bearing on the poor and bottom 40 percent, a nd how? iii.	Which of these originate from within the WASH sector and which from outside? iv.	What are potential solutions to these constraints which would significantly benefit the poor and bottom 40 percent?

Regional Knowledge Exchange Platforms One of the biggest drivers of change for parliaments is other parliaments. South-south knowledge exchange is an excellent mechanism for parliaments to learn about the institutional structure, powers and functions, and performance of other parliaments and, in turn, seek to emulate or implement similar reforms. It will explore the correlates of poverty and the drivers of inequality, distinguishing the role played by changes in demography, activity choice, occupation, labor market participation, human capital, and asset holdings.Policy Note #2 - The poverty and social impact of fuel price reforms:  This Note will look at the distributional impact of fuel subsidy reform.  Some of the questions that the Note will address are:  What is the benefit incidence of existing subsidies? How regressive are they? What are the distributional and fiscal performances of alternative targeting schemes?  The methodology underlying the Note is a mix of quantitative and qualitative approaches. The quantitative component will examine distributional performance of current scheme and alternatives using household data.  However, the universal nature of the subsidies means that there are going to be clusters of vocal and organized interests, who will potentially oppose any reforms that eliminate or reduce the subsidies. Therefore, the Note will also include a political economy analysis by collecting information from and perspectives of stakeholders. The exact instruments for engaging the stakeholders will be based on what is feasible in Nigeria.Policy Note # 3 - Agricultural productivity and rural poverty:  Agriculture remains the single most dominant sector in the Nigerian economy. It accounts for 42 percent of the country?s income (GDP) and about 70 percent of the population makes a living in this sector.  But our current knowledge of the productivity trends in the sector and the welfare of those participating in it, is limited.  This Note will fill this gap in knowledge by exploring answers to the following questions: What is driving agricultural growth? Is it skill development, infrastructure, market access, etc?  How does agricultural productivity compare to other sectors? In this Note, we shall look at the impact of climate change on cereal consumption, nutrition, health, and poverty.  Our methodology is to combine GHS-Panel data which has information on household location, shocks, consumption and agriculture production and possibly also DHS, and existing data on temperature and rainfall variation to estimate the impact of changes in these climatic variables on agricultural production and ultimately household consumption, and health outcomes. This task will extend the scope of the work being carried out by these institutions and promote broad stakeholder consultation of study findings. Please note that there was no concept paper.  BB of only $11,750 was used.  FAO and AfDB provided resources for the review.  The review was an output of the Rural Development Strategy for Nigeria.  The main report is attached. The government of Nigeria in collaboration with its development partners, in particular the African Development Bank (AfDB), International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) and the World Bank, has put in place policies and a strategy for agriculture and rural development.  The effective implementation of these calls for a strengthened and streamlined institutional framework which would assure accelerated agriculture and rural development.  Hence the development partners, AfDB, IFAD and the World Bank, have provided the resources for this review of Nigeria.s rural and agricultural sector institutions.  FAO has provided technical support for carrying out the study, which has been implemented  in two phases.  Phase I, completed in June 2002, provided a census of public institutions involved in agriculture and rural development along with their mandates, objectives and functions, and identified a number of problems and issues to be addressed to improve their effectiveness.  Phase II involved visits to 12 representative states and 24 Local Government Areas (LGAs) to review their institutional problems and issues and to provide proposals to address them.  The objective of the review is to define an institutional framework for effective and sustainable development of the agriculture and rural sector.  The purpose is to outline, as much as possible, institutional arrangements that can serve as a blueprint for planning, implementing, monitoring and evaluating agriculture and rural development projects and programmes to be supported by Nigeria.s government and its development partners. A national stakeholders workshop was held on February 9, 2004 to discuss the report and provide a roadmap for the implementation of the findings of the report. column5: 1) Firm Performance in Nigeria.  The objective of this chapter is twofold: i) compare performance across countries, and ii) identify the drivers of productivity within the country. This section will use the survey data to assess different aspects of firm productivity and sales growth in Nigeria and to compare productivity and growth of Nigerian firms with enterprises in other middle income and African countries.  This section will look at several common measures of firm productivity, including three partial productivity measures (labor and capital productivity, capital intensity) and total factor productivity.  In addition to the cross-country comparisons detailed above, this analysis will look at differences in growth and productivity measures among Nigeria firms.  In particular, the chapter will try to identify the types of firms that intensively use skilled and unskilled employment. 2) The Investment Climate.  Results from this section will come from the survey and will provide a detailed description of the investment climate.  This section will primarily draw upon objective measures of the investment climate, although it will also use perception-based data when appropriate.  Whenever possible, the data will be stratified by ownership, size, export orientation, and sector.  In addition, the section will look at how different constraints affect firms that use skilled and unskilled workers intensively.  This will provide some information on the distributional effect of proposed policy changes.  3) Labor productivity and labor markets.  This focus will explore in details the functioning of the labor market, mainly from a firm?s perspective. Given the high levels of unemployment in Nigeria, this chapter will identify the factors that are preventing firms from hiring.  Is there a skills mismatch?  Are the search costs for hiring or any other costs (labor costs, indirect costs) too high?  Is labor productivity so low that making expansion in Nigeria becomes uneconomic?  Is the labor market too segmented? Different hypothesis that may explain employment growth and labor productivity will then be detailed and finally tested.

column311: The Rural Access and Agricultural Marketing Project (RAAMP) Scale Up (SU) continues and expands support provided under the series of rural road access projects in Nigeria, leveraging the previously supported rural road asset management and its institutional framework. The project will scale-up support provided to the rural connectivity agenda in the country through the Rural Access and Mobility Project Phase 1 RAMP-1 (P072644), the Second Rural Access and Mobility programs or RAMP-2 (P095003), and the ongoing Nigeria Rural Access and Agricultural Marketing Project (P163353) financed by the World Bank and the Agence Française de Developpement (AFD), as well as the Nigeria Access to Agri Markets project, recently approved by European investment Bank (EIB).The RAAMP SU Project consists of three mutually reinforcing components to support improvements in Nigeria?s rural road network. The first will support direct rehabilitation and upgrades of 3000 km of resilient rural roads, integrating road safety consideration, and building climate resilience. The second will support climate resilient asset management, including supporting operations and maintenance of an additional 3500 km of rural roads and a climate-risk informed road asset management system. Finally, the third component will support institutional transformation and project management. Project activities also include mechanisms to support road safety management, digitalized outcome monitoring, and skills development for management of rural roads as well as gender-targeted opportunities.All states will be eligible to participate in the RAAMP-SU operation subject to meeting specific criteria to demonstrate the state?s commitment to institutional reforms and sustainable financing. Candidate roads from participating states will be assessed according to economic, social, and climate vulnerability criteria as part of the selection and prioritization process. As with the preceding RAAMP project, the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security will continue to be the project federal counterpart, ensuring project implementation at the federal level through an entity to be created within the newly established National Agriculture Development Fund. State rural access road agencies will be responsible for project implementation at the state level.

column5: Trade Facilitation in Nigerian Agricultural Markets NLTA has two major phases. First phase is focusing on private sector consultation and stakeholder organization and development, while in parallel, zooming in on detailed technical analysis to identify, in consultation with the market participants, which crops could be traded on an exchange, and what constraints in warehouse systems and in other trade, financial and regulatory infrastructure might prevent these transactions from happening. column5: The output of the project is the Subnational Doing Business in Nigeria report. The report will update the data and track the reforms of the 4 indicators published in Doing Business in Nigeria 2010 (Starting a business, Dealing with construction permits, Registering property and Enforcing contracts), across the 36 Nigerian states benchmarked and Abuja FCT.The main project milestones are:a) Presentation of the project to national and local authoritiesThe project will be initiated by presenting it to the national and local authorities of the statesincluded in the study. The event helps the authorities understand the concept and gets their buy-in and support early on. The presentation includes an explanation of the Doing Business methodology and the specific project in Nigeria. At this stage, federal and state authorities are invited to participate in the data collection and in the process overall. The national and local authorities will help identify public officials at the relevant institutions who will also complete the Doing Business surveys. The goal is to complement and cross check the information supplied by the private professionals, as well as to capture information on good practices and ongoing reforms. Potential discrepancies will be resolved through follow-ups withprivate sector contributors.b) Preparation of the Doing Business IndicatorsThe project team will work with local private professionals and government officials, as well as other local partners, to prepare the selected Doing Business indicators. The indicators will allow the states to compare their business regulations among themselves and with 185 economies globally. Doing Business in Nigeria will benchmark 36 states and the federal capital territory, including Lagos, which is measured by the global Doing Business report each year. A local Coordinating Organization will be hired to help identify private sector respondents - including lawyers, architects, construction companies, engineers, etc. # in 35 states and Abuja FCT. The organization will also hire research analysts to undertake the data collection process and administer the surveys. The research analysts will be trained in the Doing Business methodology and data collection techniques.c) Meeting with local governments to discuss preliminary findings and period of replyAfter collecting information from the private and public contributors on all indicators measured, the project team will share and discuss the preliminary findings in confidential meetings with the government of the states included in the report, followed by a period of reply. The team will analyze and review any comments from authorities with private sector contributors. Once all the differences are clarified, the Doing Business indicators will be finalized.d) Preparation of the reportThe team will then prepare a report presenting the data and the analysis, comparing the data within Nigeria and from an international perspective and providing reform recommendations. The report will be similar to other reports in the subnational Doing Business series and will be available in hard copy and through the subnational Doing Business website. It is expected that the report will guide policymakers throughout the regulatory reform cycle and will serve as: (i) a diagnostic tool to create a baseline and allow international and domestic benchmarking, (ii) a reform instrument that uncovers bottlenecks and local good practices, and (iii) a monitoring and evaluation tool to measure progress over time and create an incentive to maintain reform effortse) Launching conferenceThe report will be launched at a high-level public event with representatives from both the federal and state governments, the private sector, civil society and the media. Results will besimultaneously disseminated on the Doing Business website (www.doingbusiness.org).

column5: The development objectives of this task are to assess the current state of institutions and service delivery mechanisms in the WASH sector of rural Nigeria and to inform the Nigerian government, the World Bank Group, and other development partners working in the country on policies, strategies, and practices to improve the accessibility, quality, and sustainability of rural WASH services. In particular, this activity will aim to compare the relative strengths and weaknesses of the various modalities for WASH services provision currently employed in rural Nigeria and assess each modality on its efficacy within the five ?building blocks? of sustainability: institutional capacity, financing, asset management, water resources management/environmental health, and monitoring and regulatory oversight.  Altogether, this information will be used to inform programmatic and policy decisions seeking to expand access to sustainable WASH services in rural communities. Furthermore, this analysis will aim to capture the experiences of the private sector in Nigeria?s rural WASH services provision. Opportunities to improve service provision and sustainability through increased private sector participation will be identified based upon this analysis and through comparisons with relevant global experiences.The resulting series of analytical reports on the rural water supply and sanitation sector will be critical given the World Bank?s current support to the Government of Nigeria in development of the National Action Plan for the Revitalization of Nigeria?s WASH Sector, which intends to ensure that all Nigerians have access to sustainable and safely-managed WASH services by 2030. In pursuit of this goal, the strategy will strengthen and expand Nigeria?s WASH services while simultaneously improving their effective and sustainable management. Given the lack of comprehensive information on the various modalities of service provision in rural areas, the analytical reports are necessary to inform ongoing policy dialogue with the Government of Nigeria and support the design and implementation of a potential new project for the sector.

column5: Sector work - FY04 Nigeria Output The theme of this study is that proper pricing, removal of market distortions and forest management, supported by the right policies, can result in sustainable forestry and increased revenues for Nigeria. Given that Nigeria.s forest reserves are rapidly dwindling, the imperative now is to stem the current tide while ensuring that the policies put in place improve utilization, reduce waste of wood and ensure sustainability while contributing to the sector.s revenues.  The challenge: how to identify what forestry fiscal reform and what forest management is needed and to develop a set of policy and program proposals that both the Federal Government of Nigeria (FGN) and the World Bank can consider that would target correcting specific bottlenecks and distortions that constrain the sector. 2.   The forestry sector in Nigeria faces a constellation of problems stemming from the conflicting needs of meeting demand from the states and industry for revenue and timber respectively - all from a sector that is facing supply shortages and severe sector management problems. These problems threaten the environmental integrity of the remaining forests, jeopardize the precarious position of the forest industry and undermine the socioeconomic stability of forest communities.  These problems call for a fundamental change in Nigeria.s approach to forest management. 3.   What are the specific and overriding problems in the Nigerian forestry sector? First, forest management is non-existent and because of this the forests, even in the reserves, are degrading. Second, current revenues in the Nigerian forest sector are minimal because fees are set arbitrarily low and do not reflect the real market price of timber. Third, low timber prices and low fees, coupled with protectionist policies such as the import tax and the log export ban, mean that wood industry is inefficient and that inefficiency is subsidized at the financial expense of the state. Fourth, there is no relationship between forest planning, forest management, and the revenue system. 4.   While we know a lot about the Nigerian forestry sector through several recent studies, there is a gap of knowledge in the area of appropriate fiscal policies for Nigeria. Without an appropriate forest fiscal policy and forest management system in place, forestry in Nigeria will inevitably be unsustainable, with low benefits to the state and therefore to communities.  Correcting these problems, through better management and fiscal policies that are synergistic with the new wider policy direction of the country, can yield increased revenues to the sector, lead to sustainable forestry, and ultimately improve overall efficiency in the sector.  This report examines the Nigerian forestry sector in the context of these larger challenges and presents a coherent framework within which to develop specific fiscal reform policies and investment programs for promoting sustainable sector development.

column311: Nigeria has notably high levels of poverty and vulnerability. Predictions indicate that the ongoing global economic crisis induced by the COVID-19 pandemic has contributed to a worsening of these levels. The latest official data released by the National Bureau ofStatistics (NBS) show that around 4 in 10 Nigerians (82.9 million people) were living below the national poverty line in 2018/19. Moreover, with forecasted contraction of economy by around 4% in 2020, the poverty headcount rate is estimated to increase from 40.1 % in 2019 to 44% in 2022. This is due to a combination of the COVID-19 crisis and high levels of inflation (16. % in January 2021) with rise in food prices accounting for 63% rise in inflation. This means close to a 100 million Nigerians (about 20 million HHs) could fall below the poverty line by 2022, absent any government measures.The Government of Nigeria (GoN) is considering further expansion of its National Social Safety Net Program (NASSP)- P151488 to provide cash transfers support to the existing and new poor and vulnerable populations to mitigate the short term impact of the current and future shocks including COVID-19 pandemic and recent surge in inflation. The proposed NASSP Scale Up (NASSP SU) will complement the government plan by providing financial resources and technical support for the delivery of temporary cash transfer support to the population affected by shocks, to protect the livelihoods of the existing chronically poor households as well as by strengthening the shock responsive national social protection system.The levels of social protection in Nigeria, both in terms of financing and coverage, has been very low. Apart from low coverage, the performance of the government social safety net programs is variable is also low. The limited existing social protection programs in the country also remains fragmented. Significant and persistent gender gaps exist in Nigeria, including in access to social protection services. There has been recent progress which shows the government?s commitment towards providing stronger social protection to its citizens. The government is in the process of scaling up social protection in response to COVID-19. The establishment of the RRR and the launch of the COVID-CT required innovations on several fronts. Phase II of the project intends to expand and build upon the activities conducted through the NASSP. The World Bank has been a key partner in the government?s effort to expand and strengthen the social protection programs and systems, particularly through its support to different national programs.The overall objective of the NASSP SU is to expand coverage of shock responsive safety net support among the poor and vulnerable and strengthen the national safety net delivery system. Gender and citizen engagement are important dimension of the results to be achieved by the project. These will be monitored through the outcome indicators as well as intermediate indicators looking at specific aspects of gender and citizen engagement.The project builds on the NASSP to provide strengthened social assistance support to Nigerian citizens and will support the following components:Component 1. Economic Shock Responsive Cash Transfer (ESR-CT). column5: The last PA concluded suggesting additional analysis to clarify some contentious issues related to poverty dynamics (chronic and transient poor), the geographical distribution of poverty and the increase in spatial inequality. Data from official figures present some anomalies indicating a potential underestimation of consumption figures. The availability of the second round of the GHS and its panel structure offers an invaluable opportunity for testing a number of hypotheses. First, results from the panel can be used to shed light on chronic and transient poverty. The exercise was started in 2013 but the new available data offer the possibility of refining the analysis. At any given point in time, poverty is determined by a combination of permanent income and transitory income measured against a threshold/poverty line. Since the risk-profiles of individual households differ, poverty depends not only on the distance from the threshold, but also on a) the frequency and severity of the risks faced and b) the household?s coping mechanisms. The panel structure allows identifying chronic and transient poor and describing their general characteristics.   Second, although not representative at State level, the panel can give important indications on macro-regional trends and shed light on the overall better performance of Coastal States opposed to the expected stagnation of Northern ones. Whereas for example the good performance of South Western states-driven by Lagos- is confirmed by several indicators, more contentious is on the one hand the performance of South-South states and on the other the drastic worsening of South Eastern states.  In the event that Nigerian authorities make the census available there is also scope for constructing the first Nigerian poverty map.  Third, given the particular structure of the questionnaire for rural households, seasonal consumption of both before and after harvest can be accurately investigated. Most poor households? agricultural production is mainly based on rain-fed production systems and a single main rainy season. Many of them cannot store their produce after the harvest season and are forced to sell it when everybody sells, receiving comparatively low prices compared to selling produce in different periods of the year. Nearing the end of the lean they often run out of food and are forced to buy food becoming net buyers when prices are at the highest level. High transportation and transaction costs combined with weak market information flows, amplify all these effects. An analytical contribution in this area would help to provide important evidence on which to base social protection targeting.

column311: The CBN Technical Assistance (TA) Facility aims to strengthen the CBN?s technology-enabled and data-driven supervision and oversight across Nigeria?s banking, non-banking, payments, and remittance ecosystems. The Facility will integrate advanced data and digital tools into regulatory and supervisory processes. Beyond technology upgrades, the TA Facility supports a strategic shift toward institutional and supervisory modernization and evidence-based decision-making. The operation is fully aligned with the forthcoming FY26?32 Country Partnership Framework, which prioritizes a sound, resilient, and deep financial sector for inclusive growth and jobs, and with Nigeria?s National Development Plan 2026?2030 by institutionalizing data-driven policy, strengthening CBN?fiscal agency coordination, and expanding access to finance through more effective, risk-based oversight.Component 1: Supervision and Regulation Through Better Data and TechnologyThis component supports the adoption of: (i) Supervisory Technology (SupTech): tailored technology-based solutions that strengthen supervisory processes and risk based oversight and (ii) Digital Rulebook: a structured, technology driven solution that enhances clarity, consistency, and accessibility of regulatory framework for supervisors, financial institutions and other stakeholders. This transition will enable the CBN to become a regional leader and global fast follower in tech-enabled financial supervision. This is particularly critical given the increasing complexity of Nigeria?s financial landscape, characterized by the rapid evolution of financial services offered by institutions both within and beyond the CBN?s regulatory perimeter, including FinTech?s, digital lenders, and virtual asset platforms. Component 2: Payment Systems Infrastructure, Oversight, and ResilienceThis component supports the design of tools, technologies, and oversight frameworks to strengthen the CBN?s capacity to oversee an increasingly complex payments ecosystem, ensure robust governance and supervision of Payment Service Providers (PSPs), Mobile Money Operators (MMO) and Payment Service Banks (PSBs), and safeguard financial stability, consumer protection, and confidence in digital payments.  Component 3: Remittance Systems and Foreign Exchange (FX) Flow MonitoringThis component supports the design and implementation of analytical tools and data systems to strengthen Nigeria?s remittance ecosystem and improve the monitoring and measurement of foreign exchange (FX) flows. The aim is to deepen understanding of remittance flows, enhance the quality and granularity of FX data, and support evidence-based policy formulation and Balance of Payments (BoP) reporting. By supporting the design of digital-only remittance solutions, the component also seeks to provide insight on strategies to channel more remittance flows through formal systems.

column5: The Government is seeking technical support to identify policy actions that can enable the Housing Market to work more effectively.This task will inform the preparation of the Nigeria Housing Finance Project with three critical outputs:1. Housing Finance Policy Note - This Note will build and update the thorough analysis already undertaken as part of the recent FSAP, and the previous reports prepared under the aegis of the FSS2020 WB support. This note will bring together knowledge, data and information to provide the analytical and research underpinning for the policy choices made in the Proposed Financial Intermediary Loan.2. Housing Finance Affordability Analysis - The high level of interest rates, combined with expensive housing are seriously constraining access to decent housing for lower income and middle income Nigerians. This note will aims to identify some of the key affordability constraints and provide some reasoned recommendations on steps which can be taken to make housing and housing finance more accessible. This note will include details of experience elsewhere in the World and include a discussion of housing finance subsidy mechanisms, it will also look at other mechanisms such as credit guarantees or mortgage insurance as ways of managing risks and bringing down the cost of credit. The final area which it will cover is examining the options for pricing long term credit in an inflationary environment. Some countries have had success with indexation based pricing which makes allowances for the 'real' cost of credit rather than the nominal cost. The analysis will include a full assessment of the institutional and technical capacity to implement such a system, as well as all attendant risks both for the financial system and the consumer. The paper will be built around a financial model which will cost each option and provide detailed results in terms of affordability impact of different policy measures or combinations of policy measures.3. Description of Housing Value Chain - Multiple stakeholders are actively working on different parts of the housing value chain. Having a map across all aspects of housing would be useful as a planning exercise and as a policy tool. The CME has requested this to better understand the linkages within the sector. The note will bring together the roles of DfID and the GEMS program, IFC role, Shelter Afrique, the World Bank IDA program, the FGN, State Government and also the private sector.

column5: The Nigeria Country Partnership Strategy (CPS) for the period FY2010 -2013 developed in partnership with DFID, USAID and AfDB identifies governance as the main challenge and proposes support for: (i) effective management and accountability; (ii) participation; (iii) sector governance; and (iv) capacity development. A multi-sectoral country task team from PSRCB, PREM, FPD and HD will utilise the GPF in an innovative and integrated way to support current governance requisite activities on three cross cutting issues of transparency, accountability and participation (TAP) seen as the major challenge of governance in the country. The GPF will build on and add value to the ongoing NEITI supported by a multi-donor Trust Fund by strengthening TAP in the sector governance in oil, health and urban water. This approach will provide a unique opportunity to look at the revenue side (oil), the service delivery side (health and water) and reporting of the results in a participatory manner. There is a clear synergy in this approach of monitoring and evaluation of resource allocation/budget principally from oil revenue and how these translates into service delivery effectiveness, using case studies in health and water.In the oil sector, a typically non transparent sector, the GPF grant funds would, complement the Bank program, and International Monetary Fund support, to do the following: (a) undertake a detailed needs assessment relative to data management and transparency encompassing the entire data chain from the retrieval, maintenance and reconciliation of data files on project investment, production, costs and prices through to all fiscal assessments, production, payments, and financial flows, including funds provided to the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC) or, in an initial period, to its planned successor NNPCL, and flowing back from NNPC either as government revenues, or ultimately as dividends paid by NNPCL. (b) prioritized recommendations for future TA and implementation follow-up, including staffing and physical infrastructure (facilities, IT etc.) where possible within budget, ensure immediate consultant follow-up (c) undertake training of Nigerian professionals in tax administration as well as the monitoring and reporting of fiscal and financial flows. The TA would be primarily directed at, and coordinated with, agencies of the Ministry of Finance (MOF), the Federal Inland Revenue Service (FIRS), the Federal Budget Office (FBO), and the Office of the Accountant General (OAGF) - and the NEITI. In the human development service delivery governance consideration, it is documented that service delivery, weak accountability, lack of transparency in the use of resources and lack of responsiveness of service providers to users are major challenges that largely explain poor service delivery. Underpinning these weaknesses is the lack of voice and participation of service users in service delivery both at policy level and operational levels. These weaknesses and challenges have been highlighted by both the Country Partnership Strategy and recent ESWs in the health and water sectors. The GPF will help to build on the existing ESWs and operationalize some to their findings. It will be used to strengthen TAP in key sectors of health and urban water The activities will include design and use of tools to measure delivery, capacity building for use of citizen report cards and absenteeism surveys and publication of results; strengthening the capacity of service providers to develop and use service standards; and working with CSOs to monitor and evaluate service delivery. One state water board and two health facilities the (a hospital and primary health care centre) will be used as pilots for the exercise. The tools and the manuals will be disseminated across donor assisted programs in the Country for possible adoption.
