column5: The World Bank plans to scale-up its engagement in the North of Nigeria building on a well-informed development framework. Such a platform will identify sectors and activities that will extend the outreach of basic services to the area?s population and enhance its regional competitiveness. National convergence will be the focus of the planned activity that will address both social and spatial inequality in 15 Northern States selected as a result of a combination of criteria, including humanitarian, displacement and economic factors. The activity will consist of two key components and will address both the impact of the conflict in the North-East as well as the chronic underdevelopment throughout the 15 Northern States. Activities to be undertaken include: (a)- Component-1: Formulating an Emergency Management and Recovery Plan - Conscious of the human and social suffering in the NE, this component will address the critical emergency needs of both victims and support networks in the area (i.e. host communities). As such, this component will focus on the: (i) humanitarian and social hardship (internal displacement, injured persons, families of killed persons, individuals affected by conflict-related trauma, vulnerable populations, etc.); (ii) emergency access to education and health care services; and (iii) recovery of public infrastructure and basic services.(b)- Component-2: Formulating a development framework for Northern Nigeria and its border areas -This component will build the appropriate knowledge base needed to inform present and future Bank engagement in the region.  It will provide a deeper understanding to the background, rationale and extent of social and economic deficits in Northern Nigeria as well as the challenges (political, economic and sectoral) that led to underdevelopment, national divergence and conflict. In doing so, the component will closely review and examine border area issues and development potentials with the neighboring countries of Niger, Chad and Cameroon. It will also be guided by the active involvement of the private sector, the participation of women, and the protection of the environment and natural wealth. Finally, this component will identify catalytic and transformational socio-economic development initiatives that would leverage Federal, State and donor funds towards addressing the key social, economic and institutional challenges facing the region.

column5: Description of Activity:This activity will focus on the floods, which occurred during the fall 2012 rainy season in at least 24 of Nigeria?s 36 states. column5: The ESW will undertake a comprehensive review through three sets of studies of the state of education, skills, institutions and governance in Nigeria.  This review will incorporate, as appropriate, in-depth analysis in selective states. Study One:  This study, whose Concept Note was approved in FY13 and has since been completed, sought to explore the current status of educational attainment and key gaps. Data analysis of the National General Household Surveys of 2010-11 was undertaken to establish the basic information on the current state of education and skills in the country.  Since the mid-2000s there have been no clear data on the state of access, quality and equity information on the education sector.  Given the breadth and national coverage of household surveys of 2010-11, an account of the gross enrollment and net enrollment, primary, secondary and tertiary completion was obtained. Data was disaggregated to the level of states and regions and therefore distinguish trends across geography, ethnic and income class and most importantly by gender.  Information on the state of quality of education was also obtained from the surveys, for example on the ability to read and write for grade 3 and grade 5 students, as well as from selected studies in some states on the outcomes from school achievement tests from WAEC or NECO exams (Report No. 77597-NG:  Federal Republic of Nigeria - Education and Skills Policy Notes:  Policy Note 1:  Education Access, Equity and Quality in Nigeria).Study Two:  This study aims to explore the current skills development landscape, focusing on:  (a) the stock of skills for employability in a number of identified high potential sectors; (b) the stock of skills for improving productivity in the informal sector; and (c) mechanisms to facilitate linkages between education and the labor market. The study will look at skills development from foundation to higher levels in line with the theoretical framework proposed by Skills Toward Employment (STEP), and include not only skills but also an assessment of standards, certifications, and of the overall regulatory framework.  The full Concept Note of this study, which is being reviewed together with this Programmatic Note is attached under 'Detail Program Context' below.Study Three:  This study, ?Governance, Institutional Efficiency and Accountability,? will commence in FY14 and will be delivered in FY15. It will look at sector governance and the institutions and accountability in education from the federal level, down to the level of states and Local Government Authorities. The education system is composed of a multitude of institutions, agencies and parastatals at federal, state and LGA levels, with the primary body coordinating education through the National Council on Education, and led by the Federal Ministry of Education, comprised of the state commissioners of education. The implementation of the FME 's policies is carried out by the Universal Basic Education Commission,  22 education para-statals.  Broadly, the local government education authorities are the key players in primary education, while secondary education is under the jurisdiction of state governments with the exception of the 104 federal unity schools. Tertiary education is primarily managed by the federal and state governments, with the federal government taking the largest role, through the National Universities Commission (NUC), the National Board of Technical Education (NBTE) and the National Commission for Colleges of Education NCCE). The note will undertake an in-depth review of this structure and institutions; the governance and accountability frameworks; their financing vis-a-vis mandates and outputs; and the constraints to improved efficiency and impact. A separate concept note outlining the approach to the study will be developed at a later in collaboration PREM and other relevant units in the Bank.

column5: The transition assistance pertains to three programs that fundamentally underpin Nigeria?s trading infrastructure and revenue collection functions: (1) the Nigerian Destination Inspection Program; (2) the Information and Communications Technology (ICT) project which provides ASYCUDA++ and other IT applications and tools to the Nigerian Customs Service (NCS) and Federal Ministry of Finance (FMF), and (3) An effective monitoring/oversight unit of Customs.   All of these projects have been run by private sector concessionaires comprising four private sector companies since 2006.   The contracts, which are managed by the FMF on behalf of NCS, expired in December 2012 and their respective functions were meant to have been handed over to NCS.  The contracts have been extended under new commercial terms until such time that Nigeria can take over from the concessionaires or put in place new mechanisms to perform these critical functions.  Capacity to effectively manage these functions remains a key component of Nigeria?s fiscal and economic wellbeing.  Prior to these programs, Nigeria employed a Pre-Shipment Inspection (PSI) program and utilized an early version of ASYCUDA which was implemented by UNCTAD.  Both the original PSI regime and the new DI/ASYCUDA program were aimed at addressing issues related to trader compliance (under-invoicing), smuggling, long  clearance times, and in general, improving the trade and customs environment of Nigeria.  Since the signing of the various contracts with the concessionairs 2006, Nigeria has spent over one billion dollars on the programs. Despite the considerable investment the two programs Nigeria?s performance with respect to trade remains poor. A significant disruption in either program presents a considerable fiscal and economic risk for Nigeria and any transition from the status quo should be managed carefully and monitored. The primary objective of the Transition Assistance Program as out herein, is to ensure that Nigeria is able to effectively manage this complex transition and provide guidance and strategic input to process. A secondary objective is to monitor the transition performance to identify any potential challenges risks to the effective transition. column5: Component 1 ?Registry of Poor and Vulnerable Households -- US$170,000: The first set of activities aims provide knowledge products, manuals and templates on how to improve the targeting of poor and vulnerable households and set up a household registry of potential beneficiaries of social safety net programs. Given the lack of access to national census data with welfare indicators, the Federal and State Government Agencies and teams in Nigeria are currently using a mix of geographic targeting (geo-referenced poverty maps), community-based identification (CBI) and proxy-means-testing (PMT). The Government is also rolling out a national identity management system through the National Identity Management Commission (NIMC) and there is a strong desire, to link the national registry of poor and vulnerable households with the identity management system. Using a combination of identification methods has the advantage of minimizing exclusion and inclusion errors, and the linkage to a national ID system has the potential to greatly improve the efficiency of the program. Component 2 - Payment system for Social Safety Net Interventions -- US$110,000: Eligibility criteria, information systems, as well as effective and efficient payment systems, are key elements of a social protection system, regardless of the type of intervention. Where a single registry or unified registry of potential beneficiaries is established, the selection of beneficiaries from such a registry for targeting specific safety net interventions will depend on the eligibility criteria of the specific interventions. Currently direct cash payment using manual and non- banking systems are used on most safety net interventions in the Country. Taking advantage of the recent financial inclusion program of the Nigerian government, payment system guidelines will be developed for integration into the MIS of the Social protection system. The World Bank SP practice group?s recent work on payment system, ?What Matters in Social Protection Payments: A Guidance Note, will serve as a useful knowledge product to guide the technical assistance work on payment system for the social protection platform.Component 3 - Development of guidelines on monitoring and evaluation (M&E) -- US$80,000: This component will support the development and institutionalisation of a framework for M&E on the social protection platform. Currently a comprehensive M&E framework is been developed and tested under the YESSO. The Framework is capturing data starting from the baseline welfare situation at the point of identification and registration of poor households in the registry, to their selection and participation in social safety interventions and the long term welfare situation after exit from programs. The framework consists of monitoring and evaluation and analytical tools. Working with the relevant staff of the YESSO program and the NSSNP Team, the RSR Grant will support experts to guide the finalization of this M&E framework and the tools as well as the validation of its use even beyond interventions currently covered by the YESSO and NSSNP. Therefore this component will involve supporting the government team to develop (a) results-focused social protection M&E framework, (b) tools and templates for data collection, analysis and reporting and (c) guidelines for an impact evaluation of the various safety net interventions on the social safety net platform. South-South Peer Learning Session -- US$70,000: In the course of the implementation the RSR, the World Bank SP team will also work with other Social Protection and Labor Global Practice (SPL GP) colleagues in the Bank and the Poverty Thematic Group to organize a South South Peer Learning Session, preferably in Nigeria, to undertake cross learning and also validate some of the developed instrument and tools. The RSR budget for the Learning event (with contributory funding from other partners and stakeholders) is US$70,000.

The purpose of this study was to enhance our understanding on how to effectively engage in community-based nutrition and health programs aimed to improve maternal, newborn, and child nutrition and health outcomes, particularly in Northern Nigeria. At the heart of the analysis were case studies of four projects, each of which included a community action component for improving nutrition and health outcomes.  This report provided the comparative synthesis of these case studies. In so doing, it provided a normative base for designing and planning government programs that support reforms in outcome-based programming for maternal, newborn, and child nutrition and health through program support and investment lending.    Central to the report was the discussion on the roles played by various stakeholders # state and local government, NGOs, traditional and religious leaders, and communities themselves # in creating and sustaining community mobilization. The factors considered essential or useful contributors to community mobilization were analyzed. The history of government#s role in Nigerian health care was discussed, as well as the current situation and future possibilities, especially at state and local level.

column311: Nigeria is Africa?s largest country (over 200 million people) and largest economy (nominal gross domestic product (GDP) of around US$405 billion in 2020). Endowed with an abundance of resources and a young and dynamic society, it has the potential to be a giant on the global stage. However, with over 40 percent of its population (over 80 million people) living in poverty and a Human Capital Index of 0.36, the country harbors the largest number of people living below the poverty line and some of the worst Human Capital Indices. Foundational to this, Nigeria grapples with a daunting triple burden of malnutrition with stunting rates ranking bottom 10 globally. Nigeria accounts for the second largest number of stunted children in the world, and the largest in Sub-Saharan Africa; a quarter of the global figure of wasted children and extremely high proportions of micronutrient deficiencies. In 2024, the Food and Nutrition Security situation in Nigeria has worsened with at least 31.8 million people projected to be in crisis or emergency phases indicating household food consumption gaps in and addressing food needs through negative coping strategies. The situation confounds an already severe baseline of malnutrition with wasting rates at 7% and stunting rates at 37% and indicated to be regressing emanating from food insecurity, poor access to healthcare, climate shocks, conflict and poverty. Such a growing food and nutrition crisis threatens future economic growth by constraining human capital accumulation. Addressing this protracted development challenge will require concerted and coordinate action through a whole-of-government and whole-of society approach that tackles multidimensional drivers.The Accelerating Nutrition Results in Nigeria Project was designed as the first slice of a long-term engagement of the Government of Nigeria, to tackle malnutrition. Performance-Based Contracts supported the the delivery of a Basic Package of Nutrition Services comprising of evidence-based, high impact, prioritized interventions to improve maternal, adolescent and child nutrition. A complementary package of maternal nutrition services were rolled out through primary healthcare centres. The operation also tested the multisectoral convergence of nutrition interventions whilst incentivizing government channels for improved coordination, stewardship and accountability. The positive results from the ANRiN operation are indicative of the potential impact that could be recorded if interventions are prioritized, targeted and scaled in the right geographies.ANRiN 2.0 will draw lessons from the first operation to scale and sustain the foundation laid for nutrition programming through two components. Component 1 will focus on the deployment of a Basic Package of Nutrition Services in primary healthcare facilities and at community level. Component 2 which will scale-up multisectoral convergence interventions that promote food availability, improve household dietary diversity and build resilience across key sectors. Behaviour change interventions will straddle both Components 1 and 2. Component 3 will support multisectoral coordination and accountability actions.

column5: The Central Bank of Nigeria and the Federal Ministry of Lands, Housing and Urban Development have separately requested assistance from the World Bank/IFC in organizing a conference on Housing Finance. This will cover both the formal mortgage sector and other housing finance issues for those who are unable to access mortgage finance, and to help move the FSS2020 process into its next phase, which is implementing solutions to the problems identified in the diagnostic work. There are numerous stakeholders involved in both public and private sectors, at the Federal and state levels, in the formal credit worthy sector, and in the poorer informal segments of the population. The conference will help to catalyze a dialogue between the different stakeholders, as well as bring in experience and examples from around the World to share how other countries have dealt with some of the problems currently facing Nigeria. In particular, India, Mexico, Egypt, and South Africa all have valuable lessons to offer. The conference will also provide an opportunity for the NGO sector, development institutions and also representatives from other West African countries to share in the debate. Some of the key issues to be addressed will include: - How to move to the implementation phase of the FSS2020 mortgage plan and start creating a vibrant mortgage system in Nigeria. In particular how to address issues such as the need for long term funds or the regulatory obstacles in property registration and titling. - How to ensure access to housing finance for lower income groups, including: possible solutions for those in informal sectors; possibilities for housing micro-finance; how rental be made more secure and affordable; and whether government should support lending for lower income groups. - To bring together different stakeholders in the housing finance sector and facilitate a domestic and international dialogue, which will include sharing of international experience from countries that have faced similar problems, as well as a discussion with donors/NGOs active in the housing/financial sector sphere. This is especially relevant in the post-crisis context as financial markets seek to recover.

column311: The BRIDGE project directly supports Nigeria?s broadband strategy and digital transformation agenda by expanding access to high-quality, climate-resilient broadband infrastructure in underserved areas. With a total budget of US$1.6 billion?including US$500 million in IDA financing and US$1.1 billion in expected private capital?it will establish a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) to deploy 90,000 km of open-access fiber. Public funds will support feasibility studies, transaction advisory, SPV setup, and equity contributions. The network will be energy-efficient, climate-adaptive, and powered by renewable energy where needed.BRIDGE is designed to address structural market failures that have left much of Nigeria without reliable broadband access. It targets areas where private sector investment has not been viable, using catalytic public financing to unlock new infrastructure development and crowd in commercial capital. By improving the reach and resilience of broadband networks, the project lays the foundation for inclusive economic growth, supports digital public service delivery, and enhances connectivity for critical sectors such as education, health, and local governance.The project includes two components. Component 1: Resilient Digital Infrastructure will finance the rollout of backbone and middle-mile fiber networks, crowding in private investment through the SPV. It will fund preparatory studies, transaction advisory, and equity issuance, enabling a phased, demand-responsive deployment of 90,000 km of open-access, climate-resilient fiber. The SPV will offer wholesale services to ISPs under transparent, non-discriminatory terms, with a strong emphasis on commercial viability, environmental standards, and energy efficiency. The fiber network will replace microwave backhaul, reducing emissions and improving reliability, and will be co-located with renewable energy investments where grid access is limited.Component 2: Project Management and Implementation Support will finance a dedicated Project Implementation Unit (PIU) within the Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation & Digital Economy (FMCIDE). The PIU will oversee procurement, safeguards, financial management, and monitoring and evaluation activities. The component will also support citizen engagement, including grievance redress, and ensure quality assurance and audit functions are maintained throughout implementation.

column5: The need to develop a strategic path for agricultural development informed this technical assistance for the government ofNigeria.Agric finance is central to this strategy and the role of the government's owned Nigerian Agricultural, Cooperative andRural development Bank (NACRDB) cannot be over emphasized. Agriculture is central to increase non-oil growth and reduce poverty in Nigeria.  Agriculture contributes around 42 per cent tototal GDP and is the primary livelihood source for about 75 per cent of the population. Agriculture is the single largest sector inthe Nigerian economy. Since 2000, agricultural growth in Nigeria has averaged 5.6 percent per year, well above the Africa-wide average, but the enormouspotential of the nation's agricultural sector is still far from being realized. The improved performance of Nigerian agriculture isencouraging, but the sustainability of current high growth rates remains a challenge. The recent increase in agricultural GDPgrowth has been driven mainly by an expansion in area planted to staple crops. Productivity has remained flat, and yields of mostcrops have actually declined over the past two decades. Despite some gains in agricultural exports, for example in cocoa andrubber, agricultural commodities account for only a tiny share of merchandise exports. In contrast, agriculture was the leadingexport sector before the rise of oil in the early 1970s.Agricultural policies in Nigeria have differed over the years in terms offocus and approach, but a consistent feature has been the Government's heavy reliance on special initiatives, programs, andprojects to provide immediate solutions to pressing crises. The fragmented approach to policy-making has constrained agriculturalgrowth. Public spending on agriculture in Nigeria has been exceptionally low by global standards. Agricultural spending averagedonly 1.7 percent of total federal spending during 2001-05, lagging behind spending in other key sectors such as education, health,and water. Boosting agricultural production in Nigeria will require a coordinated strategy comprising policy reforms, institutionalre-structuring, and targeted investments to upgrade degraded rural infrastructure. The current task is a step in this directionand will assist government to develop an agricultural strategy and to restructure the Nigerian Agricultural, Cooperative and RuralDevelopment Bank (NACRDB).

column311: Nigeria is Africa?s largest country (over 200 million people) and largest economy (nominal gross domestic product (GDP) of around US$405 billion in 2020). With an abundance of resources and a young and dynamic society, it has the potential to be a giant on the global stage. But with over 40 percent of its population (over 80 million people) in poverty, Nigeria is also among the countries with the largest number of people living below the poverty line. The HOPE Program aims to support the Governments program to achieve results in human capital development in Nigeria. The operation will be open to all the 36 states in Nigeria and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT). The planned Program will be managed through a sector-wide program pooling funds (Government  and Development Partners) and     aims to providing cost effective essential benefit package of services focusing on reproductive health, maternal care and nutrition, childhood illnesses, and non-communicable disease screening. A discrete package of promotive, preventive, and simple curative interventions will be delivered at the community level, complementing facility-based primary health care services. The estimated cost of achieving full coverage of 57 primary care services under the Basic Health Care Provision Program (BHCPP) is US$14 per capita annually, more than currently available government resources. Achieving this goal will therefore require careful consideration of the pace of the planned scale-up and of service priorities. To consolidate investments, the BHCPP proposes to: (i) expand Primary Health Centers (PHCs) from one per ward to a population-responsive distribution of two per ward, on average, with a total of over 17,000  nationwide; and (ii) support the implementation of Basic and Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care (BEmONC and CEmONC), including one CEmONC per Local Government Area (LGA), for a total of 774, and an equitable distribution of Tier 2  BEmONC facilities linked to each of the CEmONC facilities. The BHCPP leverages the opportunity to strengthen emergency medical response in rural areas by addressing transportation barriers. In addition, the BHCPP includes plans for workforce strengthening, including investments in training curricula, to address personnel gaps and improve competency and skills. The BHCPP will leverage digital health to create an integrated ecosystem and supports the development of a digital backbone, ensuring interoperability and data exchange. The IPF Component will mainly finance technical assistance (TA)  that support the achievement of Program results, including: maternal mortality reduction innovation initiative to support pilot interventions to address maternal mortality in high-burden states; the hiring of an Independent Verification Agency; the design, procurement, and deployment of a federated digital-in-health enterprise architecture; operationalization of the public health fellows' program; and a platform for coordinated TA to support Program implementation. The IPF component will provide support to both national and subnational entities.

column5: The planned analytical work proposed includes several products, jointly produced with PREM. Below we describe each of these efforts. The corresponding Concept Note from PREM has additional details on the activities below.  As this is a multi-year work program, some components for FY15 might be adjusted as the work program proceeds. Specifically, in regards to the skills agenda for better jobs, the work program might grow to include a diagnostics on skills for jobs, drawing from recent work of the Nigeria Education team and its work program.1. Assessment of Jobs in Nigeria. The first product will be an overview report which is a diagnostic of the jobs landscape in Nigeria. It will present the ?big picture? of jobs and the work Nigerians do.  It will serve as the foundation for the additional analytical products in the work program. 2. Household Income Diversification. This product is described in greater detail in the PREM CN. This work entails an analysis of household diversification using the recently available panel household survey.  The analysis will focus on the correlates and implications of diversification of income generating activities from the national sample of 5,000 households. 3. Household Non-farm Enterprises. This product is described in greater detail in the PREM CN. The majority of non-farm work is in the broad category of ?self-employment?, also described as household enterprises. In Sub-Saharan-African (SSA), on average 40 percent of households rely on these activities. They can be single-person activities (a solo trader) or engaging several household members (the family kiosk in town). In Nigeria, this topic is under-analyzed due to lack of data, which can now be a focus with the GHS-panel. What do these enterprises look like? What is the scope for their growth?4. Characteristics of Wage Work. This product is described in greater detail in the PREM CN. While farming and non-farm enterprises dominate, wage employment (working for a firm, either public sector or private) is viewed as ?better? work. Indeed, statistics support this in terms of income and poverty being lowest for these workers. This product will look at the correlates of wage work and the income from that work. Special attention will be put on the labor market access for young people, women, and on the factors limiting their participation. 5. Sectoral Growth Patterns and Jobs. This product is described in greater detail in the PREM CN. This is an overview of the Nigerian labor market characteristics with respect to the main economic sectors. It will overview the country?s economic structure, the recent booming sectors such as telecommunications, trade and constructions, and implications for jobs. If the appropriate data can be obtained, we will apply the BuDDy diagnostics tool (Business Diagnostics and Dynamics) (PRMED).6. Review of Public Works in Nigeria. Recent reviews have highlighted the wide-ranging set of public works initiatives in the SP system in Nigeria, both federal and state-run efforts.  Among this set includes the World Bank?s Youth Employment and Social Support Operation (YESSO) (a $300 million line of credit), starting in 2013, which includes public works as well as training (and other aspects). The YESSO project is now operating in 8 states with ongoing public works, and will include 12 additional states. The State Employment and Expenditure for Results (SEEFOR) project is a second World Bank project in 4 additional states and has a public works component. The label ?public works? encompasses a range of workfare programs that can vary in many dimensions: duration, types of projects, and training aspects (livelihood/life skills or specific occupational skills). Under the Nigeria Jobs AAA work program, a new review will apply a Nigeria-specific lens to the global perspective on public works in developing countries. ,   Among other areas of focus, the review will examine the wide range of public works in Nigeria across a number of key dimensions such as payment setting (to what extent are they tied to official minimum wages or poverty lines), timing and duration of projects, and approach to targeting (proxy means, community based, self-selection or other methods).7. Informality, Law, and Employment Opportunities. The legal framework related to jobs is often thought of in terms of traditional labor market policies and institutions (such as employment protection, minimum wages, collective representation, active labor market programs, and unemployment insurance). However, in settings where a large share of workers are informal (broadly defined, those who are not employees or not in the formal sector), legislation impacting employment opportunities may lie elsewhere. From a gender perspective, laws related to marriage, divorce, inheritance, and land rights can influence women?s employment opportunities.  Municipal laws (such as the legal framework related to urban planning) can greatly influence the urban informal sector.  Cases studies in Thailand, Peru and Ghana done by WIEGO under the project ?Legal Empowerment of the Working Poor? (www.wiego.org) explore the relevant laws and regulations affecting informal workers in these four countries. Motivated by the large share of informal workers, as part of the Nigeria Jobs AAA work program, this study will apply a similar approach as the WEIGO case studies to the Nigerian context to understand the extent to which the legal framework has implications on employment opportunities.8. Harnessing Technology to Generate Jobs. Technology can change the way workers connect with work. What often comes to mind is offshoring jobs, such as call centers in India. By extension, there appears to be scope for such sector growth in Nigeria.  But the potential for technology to influence employment in Nigeria may reach far beyond the business process outsourcing. As described in the World Development Report 2013 on Jobs (see Box 8.5), mobile applications can provide information to jobseekers and employers or offering job counseling services. Can new ICT initiatives in Nigeria generate better work? Can a digital marketplace in Nigeria for blue-collar jobs raise incomes for the self-employed and open-up employment to the unemployed? This work will be an extension to the non-agricultural sector of the ICT work that has been on-going in regards to ICT and improving small-holder productivity.

column5: Brief of the activity:1. Undertaking Growth analytics?	Perform growth decomposition to examine determinants of growth and behavior of TFP growth.?	Examine labor productivity differences across sectors and correlate the employment growth across sectors to examine the nature of the more productive sectors.?	Assess the determinants of Nigeria?s growth over the past four decades using a Barro-type conditional convergence growth model and cross country data and estimate Nigeria?s growth potential going forward ?	Use experiences from other countries to make recommendations on Nigeria?s growth strategy going forward. 2. Undertaking Trade policy analytics ?	Analyze sectoral performance and drivers of competitiveness using national and international data (including the recent enterprise survey);?	Review government policies supporting targeted sectors and assess their efficacy ? where possible, these policies will be benchmarked against similar policies abroad or against other sectors/industries that are not             targeted by these policies; ?	Assess the economic cost of these policies, in terms of implicit subsidy elements and taxes on consumers, or opportunity costs for the economy as a whole;?	Offer trade policy recommendations derived from the analysis.Key Issues to be addressed:Growth: To date, growth has been fueled by factor accumulation (capital mostly) with only minor contribution of productivity gains and driven by agriculture sector and service sectors. Rapid growth in the services sector may be a consequence of the growth in the non-tradable sector, typical of the economies affected by the natural resource curse. The impressive growth of the 2000s, which coincides with a boom in oil prices, has not translated in a significant reduction in poverty. Growth and competitveness in the formal non-oil sector has been constrained by a number of binding constraints, notably poor infrastructure, poor business climate, and protectionist trade policies. Non-oil industrial sector has been growing impressively but still accounts for a relatively small share of the economy and has limited impact on the economy as evidence by slowdown in the economy due to the recent drop in crude oil prices. The study will address the forgoing issues by examining the determinants of growth in Nigeria, assessing the effect of trade and globalization, and projecting Nigeria's growth rate driven by both oil and non-oil natural resource.Trade: Non-oil export performance is extremely weak as indicated by the small share of non-oil exports due to the displacement of tradables by non-tradable activities through Dutch disease or resource curse effects. The government has also intervened heavily to limit competition in the manufacturing sector through tariffs and border taxes as well as non-tariff barriers including import bans. By contrast, Nigeria is relatively open to services trade and foreign direct investment but the international trading environment is challenging by poor business environments.  THe government has strongly supported prospective exporters through a number of incentive policies for exporters (Export Expansion Grant scheme,  the Pioneer Tax Program provides tax holidays on corporate income to manufacturing exporters, FTZs and export processing zones). The study will address these issues by identifying a second change occurring relates to Nigeria?s external trade policy in view of the implementation of the ECOWAS Common External Tariff and the prospect of the EPA .  It will also create pressures for doubling down on protection of sectors that are perceived as strategic to the economy.

column5: Agriculture is vital to the Nigerian economy, generating about 30% of GDP and employing nearly 60% of the labor force. Up until the late 1970s, agriculture was the main engine of economic growth, and commodities such as cocoa, palm oil, rubber, and groundnuts generated most of the country's export earnings. Agricultural exports lost steam following the discovery of oil, but farming still plays a central role in the livelihood strategies of most Nigerians. Agricultural activities are particularly important in the livelihood strategies of the poor, because poverty in Nigeria is concentrated in rural areas. Consistent with its overall policy goal of diversifying the economy away from oil, the government of Nigeria has identified agriculture as a major potential source of broad-based, pro-poor growth. The performance of the agricultural sector has been disappointing, however. Over the past 15 years, agricultural productivity has been stagnant, food production per capita has declined, and food imports have increased. The disappointing performance of the agricultural sector has been caused by a number of constraints, including inconsistent and ineffective agricultural policies, fragmented and overlapping institutions, low productivity, low profitability, private underinvestment, and a lack of competitiveness in the export sector. Following the development of the National Economic Empowerment and Development Strategy (NEEDs), the states are expected to develop their own State Economic Empowerment and Development Strategies (SEEDs). While a small number of states have made good progress in developing their SEEDS, the vast majority of states are proceeding slowly. A major cause of the slow rate of progress is the lack of local capacity to diagnose constraints to growth; identify appropriate interventions needed to overcome those constraints; prioritize the interventions on the basis of crietria such as political feasibility, likely effectiveness, cost; and develop a comprehensive and holistic multi-sector state-level economic development strategy that can serve as the basis for an implementable action plan. As part of the strategy to promote rapid and sustainable non-oil growth, the Bank in partnership with DFID is supporting a strong analytical effort to identify potential sources of growth in selected corse states, the results of which will serve as the basis for engaging governments in those states in an effective policy dialogue.

There are many ways of measuring governance and service delivery (Williams, 2011), but few apply a methodology at the sub-national level. Contributing to the debate on institutions and development, Lant Pritchett proposes to focus on state capabilities, instead of measuring Governance and Institutions to avoid the pitfall of ?isomorphic mimicry? (Pritchett, 2013). Building on Pritchett?s framework, a comprehensive assessment of state capability for a given service would focus primarily on frontline service providers. It would measure the level of efforts provided (inputs, e.g. public expenditures, number of doctor or judge per capita), and whether those leads to service delivery in quantity and of quality (outputs, e.g. number of birth assisted by qualified health staff). Outcomes would be weighted in to check to what extent outputs translates into development indicators. Users? perspectives could be used to refine data on service quality (level of satisfaction, and coping strategy such as bribing or exit). For example, a state with a large budget per capita spent in health with poor service delivery and health indicators would be ranked very poorly, as opposed to a state with lower budget per capita but comparatively better health outcomes, and no negative users views to weight in (e.g. paying bribe, or going to private health facility). Comparing capability of states, as opposed to comparing states against international best practices for institutional design, is expected to foster debates and learning between peers from different states. Understanding the role and potential change to institutions and processes would be part of explaining relative good and poor performance. Having practitioners account and justify the reasons of good or poor performance should foster effectively peer learning.  The level of complexity and granularities of the benchmarking for Nigeria will depend on data availability, states? consensus and cost. The result could vary from the very simple and light methodology of the Indian Result Framework Document to a heavier full-blown Pritchett-like State Capabilities assessment. The key aspects of the benchmarking exercise are the following: (i) the methodology should be result-oriented, and linking as much as possible inputs, outputs, and outcomes to measure state?s efficiency in delivering services to citizens; (ii) data should be consistent and representative by states to ensure comparability. Hence, the tasks during FY14 are to: (i)	take stock of data availability; (ii)	get the buy-in of the targeted states on the benchmarking exercise and the services to include;(iii)	sketch the basis for several options of assessment given available data (scenario with low, medium, high budget);  (iv)	secure the buy-in of the targeted states on the methodology options (either by involving them in an iterative process, or by validating the final proposition).(v)	pilot the benchmarking in two statesAs a point of departure Edo and Rivers States are proposed for the pilot.

column5: Background.   The two major indices of deterioration in poverty or welfare status of Nigerians in recent times is the increasing rate of youth unemployment (22%) and high maternal and child mortality ( 545 /100000 maternal mortality and infants and under-five children is 75 per 1000 live births and 157 per 1000 live births respectively) Fundamental to these two disturbing indices is the level of illiteracy or lack of functional education. 70% of the unemployed are uneducated and unskilled. Both of these cases has reached crisis situation, with the case of youth unemployment presenting a great threat to the political and social fabric of the nation.   Government at Federal and State level has shown deep concern and commitment to addressing the situation. Proposed Federal Public Workfare Program and State Government's Youth Empowerment and Employment Program, Federal Government Sustainable Job Creation Strategy, NAPEP's COPE, MDG's State CCT portion of CGS and State pilot CCTs are recent examples of government's effort in addressing the challenge and arresting the trend. The World Bank Country office has been supportive of the government effort in the policy dialogue and programme formulation process of some of the interventions mentioned above. A formal CCT lending was also prepared in 2009 but was not process because of the change in government 'borrowing plan and process'. Based on a new request, the WB, will, through a lending provide further technical and financial support to the current effort.   This lending is to support proper institutionalization and effectiveness of government's response to the challenge of youth unemployment and human capital development of the poor in Nigeria -  a 'Youth Employment and Pro-Poor Transfer Program' The YEPPT program (a 4 -5 years program) will support government effort to put in place, effective and efficient mechanisms or interventions at Federal and State levels to achieve the following:o   short term employment opportunities -especially for unskilled youthso   sustainable employment support interventions, especially for training and skills building of youths for youth friendly SMEso   protected and improved (quality) human capital of the poor and vulnerable.In response to the above the assistance would have 3 major components.o   Public works/workfare componento   Skills development and Enterprise support component ando   Conditional Cash Transfer component. column5: The  work would address the following specific areas: (A) Inventory of  knowledge on basic services to poor farmers.   The AAA would review  the services being demanded by poor farmers and, what is available on the supply side; determine the data and knowledge gaps on the issues by identifying what we know and what we do not know; and draw lessons through an assessment of what works and what does not work in bringing demand and supply together.   International best practice, trends and challenges for Nigeria in this field would also be reviewed. The AAA would answer the basic questions of- -what are the constraints on basic agricultural services whose removal can increase factor productivity of agriculture? (B) Options for effective basic services delivery to poor farmers . The AAA would  provide  a set of options for more effective service delivery based on Nigerian and global experience and the pros and cons of each.  It will assist Government in identifying priority options for the effective delivery of basic agricultural service to poor farmers. The AAA would also  seek to provide answers to the questions- - what is the nature of the livelihoods of the poor that benefit directly and indirectly from agricultural development? what are the needs of actors in the knowledge system required to support innovation and change to the benefit of the livelihoods of the poor (whether among producers, processors, traders or other support services)? How can Nigeria achieve a systemic change away from a .one-size-fits-all. approach to the organization and financing of basic agricultural services by the state and evolution within the flexibility provided for in a federal system? what are the options/approaches to supporting reforming states to find an appropriate path that allows ADPs to .do business. differently, in a manner appropriate to effective, efficient and competitive functioning of advisory services? What are the options for establishing an incentive framework for the emergence and strengthening of private sector providers of advisory services. The AAA would also seek to identify who are the champions for reforms? Who are those to be empowered with the AAA( i.e. .change agents. in government, civil society, private sector, academia, and the media). (C) Vision of basic agricultural services delivery to poor farmers . The AAA would provide a broad outline of a longer term vision of how basic services delivery should evolve. It would seek to answer three questions, viz: where we are; where we do we want to be; and how do we get there? The AAA would assist government to develop a vision for basic agricultural services for poor farmers in Nigeria. It will seek to answer the question of where Nigeria wants her basic agricultural services to be in the next 10years? Specifically, it would seek to answer the following questions: How to raise the technical efficiency of basic agricultural services? How to involve the private sector? How to ensure pluralism of basic agricultural services ( both in funding and in delivery of services? How to increase and stabilize(on a fiscally sustainable basis) the funding of basic agricultural  services? How should the roles of the ADPs be redefined in order to strengthen them? (D) Road Map . The AAA would deal with how to implement the vision in terms of the required reforms of government policy, planning and budgetary requirements, training needs, possible donor support, stakeholders roles and responsibility by integrating the analytical work and the various stakeholders  consultations and defining in very specific terms  the implementation issues and action plan. (E) Process    The process of developing  the Vision will involve representatives of all relevant stakeholders working as members of an inclusive Task Force(TF). The function of the TF will include the following: ·   Provide oversight and guidance on the overall assignment, including review of TORs, reports, etc.; ·   Promote committee work, facilitate Consultations with stakeholders and organize focused group discussions, and invite public memoranda; ·   Participate in stakeholders meetings and workshops; ·   Review and comment on consultants work; and ·   Review and comment on  draft and final reports. The proposed membership of the Task Force would be selected by the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development and inaugurated by the Hon. Minister for Agriculture. The proposed membership are as follows: ·   Permanent Secretary, Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development(FMARD) (Chair) ·   One representative of Projects Coordinating Unit(PCU), FMARD, Technical Secretary ·   One representative each from Federal Departments of Agriculture, Livestock, Fisheries, Forestry , Cooperatives, Land Resources, Agricultural Sciences, Rural Development and Planning Research and Statistics; ·   One representative each from World Bank, DFID, FAO, ADB ·   Two representatives of the Private Sector ( Input Supplier/Marketing and Processing Industry); ·   Two representatives of the NGO Community; ·   One representative from Agricultural Extension Research Liaison Services, Zaria; ·   One representative from National Planning Commission; ·   One representative of the Ministry of Women and Youth Affairs; ·   Four representatives of Farmer Organizations; ·   President , Agricultural Extension Society of Nigeria (AESON) ·   One Representative of Association of Local Government of Nigeria (ALGON); ·   Two members of the academia The secretariat of the Task Force shall be the Projects Coordinating Unit, Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development. The TF would accomplish its assignment by constituting sub-committees to work on themesAgriculture and Rural Development.  Two international consultants would be recruited by FAO and DFID to provide background working documents on basic agricultural services (i.e. where we are? Where we want to be? and How to Get there?). As part of counterpart contribution to the AAA, Government would finance part of the operating costs for the TF. However, ADB, DFID, FAO and IFAD may host some of the meetings of the TF/sub-committee meetings/focused group discussions. The procedure for consultation during the AAA work will involve a combination of approaches including consultative meetings and groupware discussions of the major stakeholders, farmers, government, research organizations, donor partners and the private sectors. The client for the AAA work is the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development. However, the assignment will be undertaken in collaboration with other stakeholders( State Governments, LGAs, Private sector, Farmer Organizations ,etc.). A national workshop will be organized during October, 2003. The main goal of this workshop is to allow the various stakeholders to brainstorm on basic agricultural  services, share the good practice experience in Nigeria and elsewhere and then develop a vision and a strategy for reform of the basic agricultural services system in Nigeria.

The activity aims to understand the increasing inequality despite consistent economic growth in Nigeria from an integrated human development perspective.  A conceptual framework that examines inequality of opportunity will be applied to applied to the education and health sector and will investigate gaps in the social protection systems in the country.  This analysis will lead to a policy note that (i) highlights the key factors associated with the inequality of opportunity in education, health and social protection, (ii) identify entry points to address these inequalities through policies and programs, and (iii) identify priority areas for support.  The activity will conduct a situation analysis that addresses the following key questions:  What do we know about inequality in Nigeria? What causes inequality to increase? What are the drivers of inequality? and what is the nature of inequality? This analysis will look at both the supply and demand factors such as unequal distribution of services as well as unequal quality of services on the supply side and information constraints, economic constraints or socio-cultural constraints on the demand side. The analysis will also try ti unpack inequality to understand its nature and the various components that interact to produce it focusing on inequality of opportunity versus inequality of outcomes where the former focuses on inequality due to factors outside an individual's control or 'circumstances'such as where they are born, their gender, ethnic group, etc.  The analysis will then look at the human development challenges in Nigeria in health, education and social protection as well as cross-cutting issues such as governance.  Approaches to address inequality will also be explored, identifying lessons learned, focusing on entry points from both supply of services and demand for services and highlighting existing program and their complementarity. Finally, the note will identify key areas for World Bank support.

column5: The ESW will undertake a comprehensive review of the state of education and worker skills through data analysis of household surveys, institutional analysis, quality of service delivery analysis, and PERs. The activities are organized into a series of programmatic outputs which will span four areas below.  The multiple outputs will be delivered as separate policy notes and with different timelines, as each of these have individual data base sources. The activity in (1) access and equity, will rely on the most recent national household survey of 2010-11 , while (2) quality of learning and service delivery will be using both the national household survey as well as the data from the quality of service delivery indicators (SDI) program as well as from examination groups from WAEC, NECO, JAMB.  The activity in (3) institutional efficiency and accountability will use results from the Grant Fund Sub-Window on improving economic governance in Nigeria, while activity in (4) on skills for employability will work with to the FPD activities in private sector, also taking advantage of the framework from the WDR 2013 on Jobs, where skills and jobs are treated dynamically.  KEY ANALYTICAL PROGRAM AREAS:(1) ACCESS AND EQUITY.  What is the current status of educational attainment and what are the key gaps? The proposed ESW will undertake data analysis of the National General Household Surveys of 2010-11 to establish the basic information on the current state of education and skills in the country.  Since the mid-2000s there have been no clear data on the state of access,  and equity information on the education sector.  The number of out of school children particularly girls in the north and boys in the east. Given the breadth and national coverage of household surveys of 2010-11, a definitive account of the gross enrollment and net enrollment, primary, secondary and tertiary completion will be obtained.  The information will be able to disaggregate the level of states and regions and therefore distinguish trends across geography, ethnic and income class and most importantly by gender.    (2) QUALITY OF LEARNING AND QUALITY OF SERVICE DELIVERY. While access have improved in the last 10 years, the quality of learning has been dismal. A preliminary look at the household surveys of 2010-11 indicates that close to 40% of the children who completed grade 3 cannot read and write.  And for the 5th graders close to 20% cannot read.  The situation has not changed or even deteriorated from 2003 when UBEC data showed low scores in math and science, only 1 % of students can achieve 50% passing. (3) INSTITUTIONAL EFFICIENCY AND ACCOUNTABILITY.   The reviews will look at the institutions and accountability in education from federal down to the level of states and to local government areas (LGAs), waht are the key constrainsts in implementation?  The education system is composed of a multitude of institutions and agencies at federal, state and LGA levels, with the primary body coordinating education through the National Council  on Education, and led by the Federal Ministry of Education, comprised of the state commissioners of education. The implementation of the FME's policies is carried out by 22 parastatals, which derive authority by legislative acts. At the local level, the local government education authorities are the key players in primary education.  Senior secondary education is under the jurisdiction of state governments with the exception of the 104 federal unity schools. Tertiary education is primarily managed by the federal and state governments, with the federal government taking the largest role.(4) SKILLS FOR EMPLOYABILITY. There is a significant misalignment of the supply of skills from post basic education and the demand fin the labor market. The operation of universities and TVET.  The study will look at linkages with demand and the private sector, and identiying skills that the education system would need to deliver.

column5: The Nigerian economy has continued to grow at a rapid pace in recent years. column5: Project Design: The NEAPD-TA activities will provide guidance for Nigeria?s access objectives by 2020 and closely integrate the technical and financial assistance necessary to achieve this goal. The two major components of NEAPD-TA, which will be carried out sequentially, are outlined as follows:(i)	Component 1: Spatial Analysis for Electricity Access - will support the development of deep spatial analysis and recommendations of the physical plan for undertaking the electrification rollout based on a critical assessment of technical and economic feasibility in two Nigerian DISCO zones. Spatial analysis is the process by which we turn raw geographic data into useful information; it includes all the manipulations and methods that can be applied to Geographic data. It adds value to the technical decision making process and can reveal patterns and anomalies not immediately obvious. The spatial analysis forms a critical part of least-cost rollout program for access expansion. This activities covered will include:-	Develop spatial model (by sub-location): Following data gathering and analysis of existing electrification infrastructure in relation to on-grid and off-grid installations, demand forecast is computed for each planning cell using a geographic information system (GIS) for the purpose of appropriately sizing the technology options to be compared in the least-cost technology model.-	Spatial prioritization for grid-compatible areas. To prioritize new grid connections, weight is given to grid-compatible cells depending on demographic and cost factors, including proximity to the existing grid; inter household distances, social infrastructure, access to road networks, and the ability of consumers in each planning cell to afford electricity. The objective of this prioritization is to ensure that the program maximizes the benefits of electrification, while minimizing program costs. New connections are identified (by sub-location) to meet the FGN?s 2020 targets.-	Spatial load forecast and review of distribution capacity. A comprehensive spatial load demand forecast is computed, taking into account the location of the prioritized new connections over the planning horizon. A high-level review of existing MV/LV lines and substations is conducted to ensure that the MV/LV distribution network has the capacity to supply the new connections.-	Comparison of technology costs. The capital and operating costs of different options for providing electricity to meet demand in each planning cell are compared over a 10-year period and discounted-into-present-value terms. The options are primarily based on grid connections and grid supply-	Off-grid electrification planning. A high-level plan can be prepared for extending electricity to locations where off-grid electrification is identified as least-cost (by programs proposed by other donor partners. (ii)	Component 2: Investment Prospectus and Access Rollout - will support the development of a detailed plan for extending electricity access that achieves FGN?s targets and by using the outcomes spatial analysis (Component 1) and describing the technical, financing, and implementation related issues in two Nigerian DISCO zones. The investment prospectus will use the outcomes and findings of the spatial analysis (Component 1) to develop a comprehensive plan covering the following:-	Background and policy. The investment prospectus will describe integration of access to energy into the wider context of a national energy sector development plan as well as the access expansion program from a higher level policy setting perspective.-	Institutional perspective. The investment prospectus will cover the readiness of sector institutions for access program and describes the measures the government will need to put in place to prepare for the access program.-	Spatial least-cost rollout plan for electricity access.

column311: The proposed FINCLUDE Project leverages the platforms of the Development Bank of Nigeria (DBN) and its subsidiary, the Impact Credit Guarantee Limited (ICGL), to drive inclusive MSME finance. Through these catalytic institutions, the Project will deploy a package of complementary, inclusive, and innovative instruments, tailored to the diverse needs of MSMEs in Nigeria. Designed as an Investment Project Financing (IPF) with performance-based conditions (PBCs), the Project comprises three interrelated components aimed at delivering inclusive and innovative financial and non-financial solutions tailored to Nigeria?s diverse MSME landscape. Each component leverages a complementary mix of market-based instruments designed to: crowd-in private capital, test market innovations, and promote financial sustainability. They include: Component 1: Inclusive and Innovative MSME Finance Products, with 2 sub-components: (i) Sub-component 1.1 : Catalytic Financing for MSMEs through the provision of Tier 2 subordinated capital to eligible Participating Financial Institutions (PFIs) and expand their capacity to lend to MSMEs in Nigeria; and (ii) Sub-component 1.2: MSME Capital Market Access to support the design, establishment, capitalization, and operationalization of an MSME Investment Fund for the provision of: (a) equity and quasi-equity financing to eligible MSMEs; and (b) long-term debt to eligible MSMEs. Component 2: De-risking and Mobilizing Private Capital for MSMEs through the capitalization of ICGL to provide Partial Credit Guarantees (PCG) for loans issued by PFIs to MSMEs. Component 3: Technical Assistance, composed of two sub-components: (i) Sub-component 3.1: Modernizing and Digitizing the Ecosystem to finance targeted TA investments to enhance structural efficiency and promote digitization and modernization across the MSME finance ecosystem. The modernization effort will focus on strengthening integration and responsiveness across the three key interrelated actors in the MSME finance chain, i.e. DBN-PFIs-MSMEs; and (ii) Sub-component 3.2: Project Management and Implementation Support to strengthen implementation capacity, including the engagement of additional dedicated technical personnel; oversight, fiduciary management, compliance, and results tracking.

column5: This activity is undertaken to implement the Governance Partnership Facility Grant to improve Economic Governance in Nigeria.  The Development Objective is to improve the development impact of public finances in Nigeria through initiatives that improve sector governance, increase accountability and effectiveness and enhanced citizen voice and participation in service delivery in key areas and sectors in the country.This activity, which is one out of six activities undertaken to implement the grant, provides for just in time governance advise, knowledge, dissemination, mainstreaming and program managementWhile all six activities aim at strengthening counterpart capacity as well as the capacity of the World Bank to leverage the Governance agenda in Bank operations, this activity will augment this aim. The activity will address the need to develop a macro level framework of the political economy of Nigeria to feed into political economy analysis at the sector and project level in the components outlined above as well as in ongoing and planned donor supported programs and projects. The component will also provide for integration of knowledge and lessons learned from the program components into the partner and client strategies and policies and provide much needed capacity to provide just in time advisory services and support on governance and political economy to counterparts and partner teams in Nigeria. The activity will seek to achieve this by providing knowledge generation, dissemination and learning. The activity will fund advisory services to ensure that gender considerations are mainstreamed into all components of the GPF proposal. Finally, the activity will provide for administration and coordination of the grant activities including the development of a solid Monitoring and Evaluation framework and log frame for the trust fund.The possibility of making the State Governors Forum a key counterpart will be explored. The following activities have been identified :i) Facilitation of a macro level political eco  nomy analysis for Nigeria and application of findings in operations.ii) Advisory services on gender mainstreaming into all components.iii) Just in time governance advisory services and support.iv) Dissemination and stakeholder involvement activities including through social media, films, workshops,conferences, web-pages, events etc.v) Coordination and program administration including monitoring and evaluation of trust fund activities.

It will focus on consolidating  existing knowledge and outcomes from recent analytical works (including from the GHS-LSMS, project studies, and Government and donor -supported works)  into a sector review which the aim of identifying prospects and actionable policies and investments for scaling up agriculture for growth and jobs, in particular among youth and women.

column311: HOPE-GOV is a PforR (hybrid) and is one of a series of three interconnected and complementary Programs strategically positioned to address different challenges, but all geared towards helping achieve the same set of ultimate outcomes. While the other two - HOPE-Primary Healthcare (HOPE PHC) and HOPE-Basic Education (HOPE-BED) will focus on the quantity and quality of services delivered at the facility level, HOPE-Governance (HOPE-GOV) focuses on the critical crosscutting challenges and enabling factors related to both financial and human resource management. The proposed Program is expected to support improvements in the strategic allocation and expenditure of resources for basic education and primary health through: (a) strengthened predictability and efficiency of financial flows and planning and budgeting processes; (b) improved transparency and accountability of financial transfers and expenditure; (c) addressing critical human resource shortfalls and improving equitable deployment. The Program implementation will involve relevant sector Ministries, Departments and Agencies at the federal and state tiers of government in  all 36 states and the FCT. The proposed Program will focus on the following result areas:?	Results Area 1: Increased availability and effectiveness of financing for basic education and primary health care        service delivery. ?	Results Area 2: Enhanced transparency and accountability for basic education and primary health care financing. ?	Results Area 3: Improved recruitment, deployment, and performance management of basic education teachers        and primary health workers.The IPF (TA) component will finance, following the World Bank procurement guidelines and regulations, a set of technical assistance activities both at the federal and state levels aimed at (i) strengthening the capacities of federal and state governments for program implementation, coordination, (ii)) Program Coordination and fiduciary management, and (iii) Verification of Results and Monitoring and Evaluation.  The first part will be the largest, focusing on providing capacity support to all participating state governments to strengthen their systems and capacities to enable them to achieve the Program Implementation. The approximate value for the IPF component will be US$ 20 million.

column282: Agricultural Extension, Research, and Other Support Activities ;Crops;Irrigation and Drainage;Public Administration - Agriculture, Fishing, and Forestry ;Agricultural Markets, Commercialization, Agri-Business and Agriculture finance ;Forestry
column311: The proposed project aims to address the critical challenges that affect competitiveness and resilience of agricultural value-chains, and thus stifle the prospects for value-added growth and job creation. In summary these key challenges include: (i) low institutional capacity and non-conducive policies that affect private sector (including farmers') participation in key value-chains; (ii) structural constraints that affect sector modernization and productivity and thus stifle private sector and farmers' returns and quality of jobs from agricultural value-chains; and (iii) poor integration of farmers to markets. The proposed project will therefore focus on interventions that directly or indirectly contribute towards Nigeria's agricultural sector modernization, productivity and value-added growth, including improved food and nutrition security in line with the country's Agriculture Promotion Policy (APP), National Agricultural Technology and Innovation Policy (NATIP). Nigeria's priorities as highlighted in these policy documents is to achieve self-sufficiency in key commodities, transform agriculture into a business-oriented sector, and ensure food security, while also promoting sustainable income and job growth. This operation will also be aligned to the Bank's Country Partnership Framework (CPF) as well as the recent aspirations highlighted in the Global Food and Nutrition Security (FNS) Program and the Mission Agri-connect.

column5: Background.   The two major indices of deterioration in poverty or welfare status of Nigerians in recent times is the increasing rate of youthunemployment (22%) and high maternal and child mortality ( 545 /100000 maternal mortality and infants and under-five children is 75per 1000 live births and 157 per 1000 live births respectively) Fundamental to these two disturbing indices is the level ofilliteracy or lack of functional education. 70% of the unemployed are uneducated and unskilled. Both of these cases has reachedcrisis situation, with the case of youth unemployment presenting a great threat to the political and social fabric of the nation.   Government at Federal and State level has shown deep concern and commitment to addressing the situation. Proposed Federal PublicWorkfare Program and State Government's Youth Empowerment and Employment Program, Federal Government Sustainable Job CreationStrategy, NAPEP's COPE, MDG's State CCT portion of CGS and State pilot CCTs are recent examples of government's effort inaddressing the challenge and arresting the trend. The World Bank Country office has been supportive of the government effort in thepolicy dialogue and programme formulation process of some of the interventions mentioned above. A formal CCT lending was alsoprepared in 2009 but was not process because of the change in government 'borrowing plan and process'. Based on a new request, theWB, will, through a lending provide further technical and financial support to the current effort.   This lending is to support proper institutionalization and effectiveness of government's response to the challenge of youthunemployment and human capital development of the poor in Nigeria -  a 'Youth Employment and Pro-Poor Transfer Program' The YEPPTprogram (a 4 -5 years program) will support government effort to put in place, effective and efficient mechanisms or interventionsat Federal and State levels to achieve the following:o   short term employment opportunities -especially for unskilled youthso   sustainable employment support interventions, especially for training and skills building of youths for youth friendly SMEso   protected and improved (quality) human capital of the poor and vulnerable.In response to the above the assistance would have 3 major components.o   Public works/workfare componento   Skills development and Enterprise support component ando   Conditional Cash Transfer component.
